speechtext: Mr. GERVAIS moved that the second report of the Select Standing Committee to supervise the official report of the Debates of the House be concurred in.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Explain.

This is the report of the Debates Committee recommending the appointment of Mr. Desaulniers as translator in place of Mr. Laferriere who died a few days ago. The Debates Committee make the recommendation to the House and hope that it will be concurred in.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that, according to the present law of the Civil Service-with which I do not profess to be familiar-this appointment cannot be made on the recommendation of a committee. I understand, however, that the gentleman who is recommended for appointment is acceptable and is to be appointed, but by the regular authority that has power to deal with such matters under the law.

Inasmuch as there is a divergence of opinion, as I understand it, as to the competent appointing body, would it not be well to have the matter looked into? As far as I am concerned, if the Committee on Debates is only an ornament, not being much of an ornament, I must decline to continue to act on it; and I am satisfied that that is the feeling of the other members of the committee. If one committee of this House can engage a young professor to perambulate the country for another purpose, I cannot see why a standing committee of this House should not have the authority to recommend the appointment of an officer to carry on the work of which that committee has charge.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I can only say to my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) that I should be sorry to lose his services on this committee. I could better dispense with his services in some other matters. He is right sometimes, especially in military affairs-

This is not a military committee.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER-and I understand that, in this case, the gentleman he recommends is quite acceptable.
That is not the point. This is a question of principle-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is it; have we or have we not this power?
That is what we want to find out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that the authorities deny that we have the power.
Would the Prime Minister mind giving the authority to the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It_ is provided under the Civil Service Act7

The Act provides how appointments shall be made to the Civil Service. And, while, as I understand it, it was not intended to take from the House any of its rights in the management of its affairs, still it was agreed that appointments should be made according to the Act, and 97}
by the same authority that makes appointments in other portions of the Civil Service-that is, the Civil Service Board. If that be correct, I do not think that this is the way to do it. This involves a charge on the revenue, and is not in order for that reason. But there is the other objection that appointments are to be made by the Civil Service Board and not on recommendation of this committee.

Under the Civil Service Act, action with regard to the appointment of an officer of the House of Commons must be taken by the House of Commons. And, in the case of the appointment of an officer of the Senate, action must be taken by that House. I understand that, by the passing of the Civil Service Act, the House has not been deprived of its power of expression which it gets from the. law of nature and not froni any enactment. And it has power to express itself to the Civil Service Commission in relation to an appointment. The Debates Committee are simply making a recommendation to the Civil Service Commissioners that Mr. Desaulniers be appointed; that is all we are now doing. If the appointing commission do not want to deal with our recommendation, the time will come to decide whether their action is legal or illegal, right or wrong. But I do not think for a moment that the House of Commons should refuse to recommend a first-class man, who has passed his examination three years ago-"before the Board of Civil Service Commissioners was established- and come out of the examination with the highest marks, who has been on the waiting list for three years and has been employed as spare translator at an occasion during that time, and who also is declared by the government as perfectly capable of doing his work. We propose, that, and I think the House of Commons should express its opinion that Mr. Desaulniers will be a fit and suitable person to be translator of debates. It will rest with the Civil Service Commission to accept the expression of opinion of the House of Commons. That is. all we are asking of the House. We may make the recommendation-
I would like to ask the hon. member (Mr. Gervais) a question. He recommends to the House thus and so; the House agrees to the recommendation- is not that practically carrying it into effect?

It is not the same thing at all. Under the new Civil Service Act, the commissioners may declare that our recommendation is not in conformity with all the requirements of the formalities provided for under the Act, and may refuse to accept our recommendation. That will .end

the matter, unless some other action is taken by this House. But I do not see why this Debates Committee, entrusted by this House at the opening of the session with the supervision of the official report of the debates, should be treated in this way. If so, there will be only one thing to be done, and that is for every member of the Debates Committee to hand in his resignation. We are making the recommendation; that is all. We are simply making a recommendation, which we thought the Civil Service Commission might accept or ignore.
To settle the question, I rise to a point of order. I ask your ruling, Mr. Speaker, if this motion is in order in the face of the law.

Although I am a member of the Debates Committee, I was not present when that recommendation was adopted, and I think the committee has not taken the proper step to obtain the appointment of a translator. I understand that the translators of the debates are governed by the Civil Service Act and that they are under the control and authority of the Speaker as head of the Department of the House of Commons. According to the Civil Service Act, I understand that the head of the department, on the certificate of the deputy head, who in this case is the clerk of the House, may ask the Civil Service Commission to appoint such an officer, and, thereupon the Civil Service Commission has power to appoint him, and this in accordance with section 21 of the Civil Service Act amendment, with or without examination. I have no doubt that Mr. Desaulniers who has passed the required examination before the Civil Service Act was in force, if appointed, would fulfil the duties of the position satisfactorily. But I do not think the proper course under the Civil Service Act is for the Debates Committee to recommend the appointment of such an officer. I think this is a case in which the Civil Service Act must apply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Might I suggest that instead of asking for the ruling of Mr. Speaker, we might accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Victoria and Hali-burton (Mr. Hughes), that, if there be a doubt as to the legal interpretation of the Act, we endeavour to have that doubt removed by obtaining the opinion of the Department of Justice. Happily, there is no difference of opinion as to the man recommended. The understanding, however, is that the House has agreed to permit its officers to be treated in the same way as officers of the Civil Service; and in the case of a technical officer to be appointed under the Civil Service Act, the commission would have to be satisfied that he was qualified, and* that the nature of his services came Mr. GERVAIS.
within the scope of the class to which it was proposed to appoint him. Applying that rule to this case, it is suggested that the Civil Service Commission must deal with this application.
Under the law, how could the matter be bi ought before the Civil Service Commission? We must look at that commission through smoked glasses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not wish to interpret the law, but rather to act upon my hon. friend's own suggestion. This same question may come up again, and it is as well that we should have a clear understanding of the application of the new Civil Service Act to the officers of the IJouse of Commons. I would therefore suggest that my hon. friend do not press his motion today; and as we all have the same object in view, every good end will be served by adopting the suggestion which has been made.
Acting on the suggestion of the Minister of Finance, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let the motion stand for another day.
Let it stand for another day.

Wherever in one of the departments an officer is to be appointed by order in council, similarly, an officer of this House; but as an order in council can only appoint a person who has been recommended by the Civil Service Commission, so this House can only appoint one similarly recommended. I do not know anything about the action of the committee. In one sense it may be all right, but still I think it is extremely desirable that the provisions of the law should be observed, and I concur entirely in the view expressed by the Minister of Finance that the opinion of the law officers of the Crown or of some legal authority should be obtained for the guidance of the House.
I take it that that opinion will be communicated to the House when it is obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The clerk of the House will comply with the wish of the House in that respect.
Motion withdrawn.

TEMPLEMAN moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 132) to amend the Gas Inspection Act. He said:	The
most important amendment is in section 3. Under the present law there is a percentage of allowance made for errors in the inspection of meters. That percentage is reduced,

thereby assuring greater accuracy in the meters in use. It is largely on the recommendation of the officers of the department and the city of Toronto that this amendment is proposed. Under 'another amendment power is taken to test gas for its calorific qualities. At present it is tested only for its illuminating qualities. The other amendments are not very important. In several clauses the word ' district ' is inserted in place of the words ' city, town and place,' as the work of the department is regulated by districts.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before the orders of the day are taken up, I want to ask if the Allan line of steamers, which have a subsidy from the government for carrying the mails via Havre, have given up calling at Halifax. I should like to know whether they are compelled to call at Halifax or not

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry 1 cannot give the information at the moment, but will get it on Monday.
I might say that the last Allan steamer, the ' Corinthian,' arrived at St. John the day before yesterday, and did not call at Halifax.

The following clipping has been sent me, taken from the Toronto ' Globe ':
Arrangements are being made, says the London ' Daily Mail,' bv which a number of boy scouts will be enabled to visit Canada during the ensuing summer, and so have the opportunity of practising scouting under conditions which would be impossible in this country. *
Red Indians will be employed to lay trails and also to teach the boys the art of tracking on a scale which could not be attempted in England. Canoeing, fishing, and following the slot of the wild deer will also form part of the scheme, which is a sequel to the interchange of the visits between English and German boy scouts last year.
The boys, who will be under the care of scout-masters, and for whose welfare the most precise arrangements will be made, will be selected by competition. The trip will be quite free of cost to the participators.
Has the Minister of Militia any information concerning this?
I have not. This is the first I have heard of it.

Owing to the regrettable illness of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), I addressed about ten days ago a letter to the deputy minister asking for application forms for fish fry. I have not yet had a reply, and should like to know to whom I ought to address a communication in order to get a reply within a reasonable time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am surprised that the hon. gentleman has not received any answer. I shall make inquiries at once.

Has the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) any information yet aa to whether a decision has been come to by the United States authorities to admit Canadian exports under their minimum tariff, or whether he has had any communication at all with these authorities on that subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are only aware of what is currently reported in the public press as to the proceedings of the United States authorities in these matters. I have no official information.

Might I ask when I may expect a return to an order of the House of December 6, promised for the early part of last week, respecting the number of officials of the Senate and House of Commons, who have residences supplied them by the Crown?

When will the report of the International Fisheries Commission be laid on the table? I see by a despatch from Washington that President Taft has trans-mited the report of Professor Starr Jordan to congress.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend refers to the commission about the international waters and lakes. This report ought to be laid before this parliament and congress. It has been laid on the table here.
House in Committee of Supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before my hon. colleague the Minister of Railways proceeds with his estimates, I would ask the approval of the House to a proposal to grant the sum of $50,000 from the treasury of Canada towards the fund organized in France for the relief of sufferers from the recent floods. We are glad to know, from the latest information, that the waters are receding and conditions improving. Nevertheless, the information available to us, both official and unofficial, shows that there has been very great distress and misery, and that there is much need of relief. Generous citizens of all nations are contributing, and in some instances governments have contributed. I am sure it will be the wish of this parliament and the people of Canada, irrespective of class, creed or nationality, that the Canadian people should show sympathy with the government and people of France in this trying moment. I propose that we should ask the French gov-eminent to accept the sum of $50,000 as a practical expression of our sympathy and desire to assist the suffering.
Could the minister give us an idea of the losses and the degree of distress being suffered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is difficult to obtain anything like an official estimate. We have to rely to some extent on the public press. We have communicated with our Paris agents to ascertain whether foreign contributions would be desirable and acceptable, and we are assured that such contributions will be gladly accepted by the French government. What wre intend is that this amount should be forwarded to the French government through our Paris office and the British ambassador at Paris, who has kindly consented to communicate with the French authorities.

This is a course which has been taken more than once where the people of foreign countries have suffered from great disaster, and it seems to me eminently fitting that a similar course Mr. BLAIN.
should be followed in this case, more especially as the country to which this offering is made is the ancestral home of a very considerable part of our population. It is also appropriate for the further reason that the relations between the British empire and the French republic are at present of the most cordial and satisfactory character, as we believe they will continue to be in the future.
Would the minister state whether some other governments have contributed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, our Paris office informs us that the government of Turkev has contributed $10,000 and New Zealand $2,500. I think the United States government is contributing in a less formal way, and judging from the public press, through the Red Cross Society very large sums are being contributed by individual citizens of the United States and foreign countries. I notice that the German Emperor has sent his personal contribution of $5,000, but at the moment of our latest information the only governments to contribute are Turkey and New Zealand.

Like the Minister of Finance, I believe in charity being the greatest virtue, but while I do not want to speak in any way against what he has brought before the House, I want to remind him that charity begins at home. I have brought to the attention of the government on various occasions cases in my own riding where, owing to floods, farmers have not been able to reap the benefit from their operations which they should reap." No attention whatever has been paid to that bv the government, and I want to again impress on the government that, we ought to take care of our own people whenever we have an opportunity. In saying this I do not want any one to misunderstand me or to think for a moment that I desire to do anything less than the Finance Minister in aiding these poor unfortunates in France.
I believe, Sir, that charity, while a good thing, ought to be reciprocal at all times. We all remember of the disaster here in Hull and Ottawa in 1899, when so many of our French Canadians were left absolutely destitute on the_ streets as a result of that fire. At that time various nations of the world came to our aid. I shall give a summary of the cash subscriptions that were sent from various sources to aid the Hull sufferers. They were as tollow's:

I hope that the government will remember at this time the action of France at the

time of that disaster and reciprocate to the very fullest extent the kindly aid we received from the motherland of the ancestors of the people who were the sufferers from the disaster I spoke of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My friend has laid down two principles, neither of which I entirely concur in. In the first place, in the sense in which he uses the words, I cannot agree with him that charity begins at home. It is particularly the business of the Dominion of Canada to attend to the giving of foreign charity if a case may be worthy of charity, but the government of Canada is not a body for distributing charity at home. We have organizations, provincial and municipal, for the granting of charity at home, and the fact that the Dominion government did not grant charity in any particular case where disaster has arisen at home would by no means be evidence that the Dominion parliament was lacking in liberality or had in any respect failed in its duty. We are the proper dispensers of charity for a foreign country if Canada desires to give such charity, but this parliament is not the proper dispensing body for charity at home.
Are we to understand that the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) is to apply to a foreign government for charity in his locality.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; but I have such faith in the provincial and municipal organizations of Manitoba that I would say that with these provincial and municipal organizations, in 19 cases out of 20 there would be no need of any foreign charity assisting the people of that section. But if there be any exceptional and unusual case of need, then it is a question whether the Dominion parliament shall grant it. We have sometimes had embarrassing questions as to whether we should grant relief in the cases of fires in Canada, and I think on the last occasion when we were considering a grant of that kind, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) pointed out, and reasonably, that it was very difficult to lay down any principle upon w7hich we should aid funds of that kind from the Dominion treasury. However, if there should be anything of that kind exceptional and unusual, I have no doubt the parliament of Canada would respond.
My hon. friend's second thought was that charity should be reciprocal. 'And now abideth faith, hope and charity, but the greatest of these is charity.' It does not add that it must be reciprocal; charity must be voluntary in every case.

I do not subscribe to the principle that charity begins at home
in such a case as this. There is but one idea that should animate the human breast in making gifts of this kind, it is that of humanity. A great calamity has happened, humanity is suffering, humanity is in need and I think that neither relationship, nationality or anything else should actuate us beyond the tie of human brotherhood that binds us to the human race. I think it should be given on that line and on that line alone.

I do not propose to say anything against the resolution introduced by the Minister of Finance. If there is suffering and want in Paris because of the unusual floods that have taken place, there, it is quite proper for the Dominion government to give out of its plenty something for the relief of those sufferers. But I wish to call the attention of the government to a case in my own county-not that I want to ask for any charity from the funds of the Dominion of Canada for the people in a portion of the county of Frontenac, but I want to asx for consideration of the rights of the people of the township of Bedford who suffer every year owing to floods caused by a certain government dam, known as the Wolf Lake dam. These people have had to meet the damages thus caused, and I think that this is a proper occasion to call the attention of the government, and particularly of the Minister of Railways, to this case.
I would like to ask whether the Prime Minister has considered this question? This must be, unless there is a string to it, a severe jolt to the autonomy of which the government speak.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I fail to see the joke.

It is not my intention to take any exception whatever to the grant of $50,000 to aid the sufferers in France; but it has occurred to me that possible we ought to learn some lessons from what has occurred in the old lands which may be useful to us in this country. If. the flood has been caused, as some suggest, by the meandering of the comet which has been roaming around the world for the last 70 or 80 years, of course we can take no action, we cannot defend ourselves. But it is alleged that the clearing away of the forests in the north of France, where the river takes its source, has largely been the cause of the flooding of the country. Rains were plentiful, and there was nothing to hold back the water. The natural forests had been cut away, the result being that the water came down with greater rapidity, and caused the overflow w'hich has brought about so much trouble. Now, in this country are we doing our part

to prevent an occurrence of that kind? Is it not a fact that we are not taking measures to prevent such a thing? I have no doubt that it is felt throughout the province of Ontario that the waters in the spring of the year come down much more rapidly from the unorganized districts to the lakes, and cause flooding, which would not take place if the forests were maintained. I think there is a lesson here for one of the commitees of the House which has to deal with the conservation of our natural resources. I have heard it said, and I presume correctly, that the reasons for the floods in France has been the cutting away of the forest around the sources of the river. If that is the case, I think there is a lesson for us, to take warning, because we might not find France and other countries so willing to come to our aid as we, in our good heart, propose to come to the aid of the people of France.
Prince Edward Island railway-branch line Harmony to Elmira, $150,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways).
speechtext:
This branch line wa3 undertaken two years ago. It is ten miles in length, and is estimated to cost $315,000. The House will remember that I gave the estimate off-hand at something like $400,-
000.
Does this complete?
No. We have spent on it so far only $25,000, and we are asking $150,000 to spend this year.
The minister might read some of the larger items, showing the rates upon which they moneyed out the different quantities.
Common excavation, including material, 17 cents; solid rock, $1.10; loose rock, 17 cents; foundation excavation in water, 70 cents; foundation in air and water, solid rock, $1.50.
That would seem as though it would cost $135,000 the way they moneyed it out. Where does the minister get the difference between that and his estimate of $315,000.

I am giving the estimate of the engineer on the $315,000. He makes an estimate as to what it will cost, and that is the engineer's estimate. The contractor comes along, and he makes an estimate of $135,835, that is, for the quantities only in the contract. The other includes rails, clearing, close cutting and grubbing. $315,000 includes all these things.
Will the minister get it down to what is included in the contract or estimated for by the engineer and see how it moneys out? I want to see how near the engineer came to the contractor's price.
The estimate for the items in the contract as made by our own engineer is $139,506.40 and the tender is $135,835. The items estimated for the balance amount to $176,016.
What is the gauge?
It is a narrow gauge.
Who has the contract?
Whitehead Brothers, the lowest tenderers.
That would be about $40,000 a mile for a narrow gauge railway.

I always like to be safe. The estimate given by the engineer is $315,126, considerably less than I mentioned last year. Tenders were asked for in the usual way, and these were received, at these amounts: $142,911; $175,219; $146,036; $148,811; $135,835. The latter was received from the Whitehead Brothers, who got the contract. It was awarded on schedule pricae. I am giving what they called the quantities moneyed out by the engineer. His estimate was $315,126.
Has the minister the estimates of the quantities so far as they have gone?
The work is only starting, we have not yet much data of the quantity, and how it will work out.
Progress estimates, I suppose, are paid upon the certificate of the resident engineer?
Yes.
Who is the engineer in charge there?
Laurence is his name.
Is he a Prince Edward Islander?
Yes, he is a Prince Edward Island man under Mr. McKenzie at Moncton.

I would like to call the minister's attention to this fact that if, when these tenders had come in he had asked for the estimates in the office, he would not have to make them up here. Does the minister, when he is letting a contract, inquire what the engineer estimates the work to be worth?
Every detail is set out in the order in council, and I have it all in my hand.
Does tire contract fix a time for the completion of the work?

The contract fixes a time, but, as in most, cases, the time under the contract is likely to be extended. We usually fix, approximately, the end of the year for which the vote is taken. This amount will not finish the work; the whole estimated cost is $315,000.
How much has been paid to the contractors up to this time?

Engineering and everything else has cost $28,618, of which practically all but $1,000 has gone to the contractor.
Increased accommodation at Charlottetown, $79,320.
This finishes the work. The entire item is a re-vote. The amount to be spent is not so much as originally intimated.
What is the work?
Additional sidings, new rails, stone-filling, concrete curb, new 20-stall engine house, and items of that character.
Who has the contract for the engine house?

The contract was awarded to Clark & Morrison, the lowest tenderers for $44,400. The contract for the freight-sheds was awarded to Mr. Clark of Sum-merside, at $8,140; the turntable to the Canada Foundry Company.
Had there been a turntable there before?

Yes. It was removed to some other place and a new one put in.
Georgetown-engine-house at-$5,000.

This is absolutely new. There has not been an engine-house there up to this time.
National Transcontinental railway - surveys and construction, $27,000,000.

This is a vote for the Transcontinental Commission. The amount asked last year was $20,000,000. I laid a statement on the table the other day carrying every item of expenditure practically up to the end of the calendar year, 1909, and showing a total expenditure of something over $15,000,000. The statement showed also the amount of work that has been done on the eastern section this year, and the amount done up to date.
How much was spent on surveys in 1909-10?
I laid on the table a duplicate of the statement I have now before me.

We have not seen it. Of course, the minister must
know that we require a statement of the expenditure, and how it compares with the estimate, how much work is done, and how much remains to be done. We do not ask for details, but we do need totals of the several items.
If my hon. friend (Mr. John Haggart) would consult the copy of the report which I laid on the table, he would have the matter pretty well in hand.
We have had no opportunity to look at it, even if we had seen it. It would be better to let the item stand, or, at least, some item on which we may be allowed a full discussion later on.

That is unreasonable. But this interim report is merely for the accommodation of members of the House. The report required of the commissioners by law is the annual report, and that I laid on the table almost the first day of the session.
But of the work for nine months we have had no information whatever.

That is the way the matter' is left by the requirement of the law-[DOT] that the work done for the year ending March 31, shall be shown in the annual report. But, for the convenience of the House, I gave this interim report of which I have spoken, and I gave amounts also in the statement made in the House the other day.
In that statement, the minister gave figures only for the fiscal year.
No, in many cases the statement was brought down to December 31, 1909, and in others to November 30.
In the estimate now under discussion, there are two items-surveys and construction. How were they divided in last year's expenditure?
In engineering and supplies, $6,935.59. The rest went to construction.
How much of the $20,000,000 has been spent?
Altogether $15,939,985.67.
Did I understand the minister to say that the statement of expenditure for the nine months ending the 31st December, 1909, has been published?

No. The commissioners must make a report annually at the end of the fiscal year. I asked for an interim report, which would show what has been done for the nine months, but that is not published unless the House so orders.
This is the first I have seen of this statement. I have not had an opportunity of looking at it.

I have been rushing to get all the information possible, and the reason I am bringing these estimates so early is that in the peculiar position in which I am placed, I want to get them through while my deputy is with me, for the new deputy would not know anything about them.

So far as that is concerned, this interim report is practically non-existent, because nobody can examine it for the purpose of making any criticism or any recommendation. No one would desire to embarrass the minister under the peculiar circumstances in which he is placed; but as a matter of fact, the construction of the Transcontinental Tailway is not especially under the charge of the deputy minister, but is under the commission appointed for that purpose; so I would not think that the absence of the deputy minister would make a great deal of difference in that regard. At all events, I think the item had- better stand for the present.

I have no objection. 1 placed a copy of this statement on the table oi the House.
Item allowed to stand.
Hudson Bay railway-to provide for the survey and location of a line of railway from the Saskatchewan river to the Hudson bay, $180,000.

This item is only to com. plete the location of the line. Although there is a difference of opinion as to the better harbour, the location of the line for 260 miles from the Pas to Split lake is a common location, no matter which harbour is selected. This item is for the location of the line up to this point. When that is done, we may possibly have the other question settled.

What are the proposals of the government with respect to construction? Is the railroad to be constructed by the department, or is it to be let by contract, or is a charter to be given to some private corporation?

I expect to bring down an item for construction in the supplementary estimates, when I hope to be able to give the information which my hon. friend asks for. A bridge is to be constructed across the Saskatchewan at the beginning of the line, which would have to be done whether the work were given.to a company or carried on by the government. It would not affect this item, which is merely for the survey and location of the line.
What is the total cost of the survey? .

Has the minister anything to tell us with reference to letting the contract to Mackenzie and Mann? It is stated in the press that the government is about to let the construction of this railroad to that firm, and that Mr. Mann was down here the day before yesterday. Perhaps the minister would tell us whether that is well founded or not, and how far the negotiations have gone.

Mr. Mann was down on some other business. He did not discuss this with me at all. We have no agreement with any one for the construction of this line. It is absolutely an open question, so far as I know.
Is it the intention to construct a portion of that line this year?

It is the intention of the government to start construction, and I hope to give more details when I ask for an appropriation for construction. A bridge might be constructed or a portion of the line, but whatever may be done will only be to save time and not delay the work. If the work be given to a company, whatever be done can be taken into consideration in any arrangement made.

I understood the hon. minister the other day to say that Mr. Armstrong had demonstrated that Nelson harbour was a very superior one. I do not find that to be the case. The remarks of Mr. Armstrong are not based on his own surveys, but on various reports issued by the Department of the Interior and on information supplied by Hudson Bay Company officers. If that i3 all there is in Mr. Armstrong's report, for which we are paying all this money, I am afraid we are not getting much in return.

Mr. Armstrong has made a report since the departmental report of March 31, 1909. He made a later report in a small volume which was laid on the table some weeks ago, and accompanying that report is a chart showing the soundings taken by Mr. Armstrong himself.

Is it not a fact that the Canadian Northern has a line constructed as far as The Pas, and has not the government an idea of that company undertaking the construction of the road? If not why has the government selected The Pas as the starting point?

That seems to be the natural point at which to start. It is the nearest to the existing system and to Hudson bay, and the idea of the government was to make connections from the nearest point to Hudson bay.
Any other system would have to go near it too.
The total spent on the survey is about $157,000. That will be to the end of the year.
Does that include the vote you are getting this year?
No.

What is the total
cost?
The amount this year and the amount already expended would be a little over $500,000.
Is not that an enormous sum for the purpose of locating a road like that?
My deputy says it is very moderate. It is really an investigation during the last few years, instead of location. The country is pretty far from home.
That amount is all practically for preliminary surveys?
The $180,000 we are asking for location, and the $187,000 for preliminary surveys.
Who has control of this, and who is responsible?
Mr. Armstrong is the engineer directed by the deputy minister, and the business management is under the deputy head of the department.
Who makes the appointments?
Mr. Armstrong himself, and Mr. Butler together, selected the men for the different parties.
Who buys the supplies?
Mr. Armstrong.
How are they bought?

The great bulk are
bought from the Hudson Bay Company because that company has better facilities for delivery than any body else.
What supervision is there as to accounts and prices?
Every account is checked by the chief engineer or some one under his charge.
Is there any departmental audit?
Yes, there is a very careful departmental audit of everything. Mr. Bell is the head of our audit department, made so under our reorganization.
Are none of the supplies purchased by tender?

I am informed that wherever practicable tenders were called for
and prices obtained from different parties and the lowest taken.
Quebec bridge construction, $1,000,000.
I imagine that hon. gentlemen know a good deal about the situation of this bridge.
Is it possible to state when the bridge will be completed?

I said the other day that I thought it would be at least four years from the time the contract was let. The contract cannot be let until next aut umn, and I am of the opinion that unless greater progress is made, and that is not likely while parliament is sitting, this $1,000,000 will be all we will be able to spend in the meantime.
At what time does the contract call for the completion of the foundation piers?

One next fall and the other the year following. There are two piers which will be required whether it is a cantilever or a suspension bridge. Another will be required if it is a cantilever. This is included in the Davis contract, but the contract is so drawn that it can be struck out if it is not required.
What if the old foundations are not being utilized?

One pier in its entirety. The foundation of a very large pier is being used on the south side but it will be enlarged. The old pier was 150 by 50 feet and the new one is to be 180 by 80 feet. They have taken it down to low water mark and are using the foundations and enlarging them.
When does the minister expect to have Transcontinental railway trains running in Quebec? That is of great interest to the maritime provinces.
The railway from the east will be constructed before the bridge. I think it will be at least four years from the coming autumn before it is completed.
What about the Transcontinental trains to Quebec?

I am informed that if it is found advisable a ferry can be established to carry quite a number of cars at that point. There is a car ferry now between Quebec and Levis, with provision on the boat to meet the rise and fall of the tide.
Can the minister give details as to the estimated amount which will have to be expended on the bridge and its approaches?

The other day my hon. friend (Mr. J. Haggart) estimated that the bridge would cost between $8,000,000 and $10,000,000. That is money yet to be expended. My own opinion, without being absolutely tied to this figure, because everything is not completed to make a full estimate on, is that my hon. friend was perhaps $1,000,000 under the right amount, that we will have to spend $11,000,000.
Not including what you have paid to the Quebec .Bridge Company.
No.

I would like to understand the situation with regard to the piers. I understand that the superstructure of the bridge gave way from some defect in design and was precipitated into the water and remains there. I was not aware until the minister made his statement a few days ago, that there was anything wrong with the piers.
No, there is absolutely nothing.
Then why have they to be increased or strengthened?

My hon. friend struck it in his opening remarks. The piers of the old bridge were too light. The new structure will be nearly twice as heavy as the old one, and the piers have to be enlarged to meet the new design.

It amounts to this, that the piers were quite sufficient for a bridge which would fall down, but they are not sufficient for a bridge which is to be permanent. The design of the piers was wrong, because the design of the superstructure was wrong.

We are very much interested in the east in the construction of this bridge. The minister says it will take about four years to complete it. Is it the intention of the railway to facilitate transportation in any way by means of a ferry across the St. Lawrence? Do the government propose to help us out in that particular, and is it not possible to press the work along and bring it to a conclusion within four years?

My hon. friend will see that I am very careful in what I say. While we want the bridge done as rapidly as possible, a structure of this magnitude must be done very carefully. I think there is brought to bear on it as fine a quality of engineering skill as there is in the world. These men will only go so far as they can feel their way at every inch, because it is something new, nothing like it has ever been undertaken.
Is it a suspension or a cantilever bridge?

This design is a cantilever. I had hoped to go to Quebec and look over that ferry, as they use it now. But my experience of the Intercolonial convinces me that we cannot hope to carry traffic by a ferry as well as a bridge. Bu't it will do until the bridge is constructed-
The minister has not answered the question I put, as to when he expects Transcontinental trains to be running from the west to Quebec.
I am not in a position to answer that. My hon. friend asked me when I expected trains to be running from the east into Quebec in connection with the bridge.

No, I said trains running from the west to Quebec, or from Quebec to the west, because this bridge is a very important link in the system' upon which the eastern provinces are depending. If, in the meantime, traffic is going to be carried by the Grand Trunk to Portland, Maine, and it gets settled in that channel, it will be very difficult to get it back to the maritime ports.

I would not like to say when the Transcontinental would be running into Quebec. We are making fair progress with the construction. But I would not care to express an opinion, because I cannot do so upon any authority.
Will it be before the completion of this bridge?
I imagine it will.
Is that road liaulipg wheat now from Winnipeg to Port Arthur?

I think not. Mr. Gordon Grant informs me that, except for speed of the trains, which, of course, is of great importance in the present transportation problem, they are using the road now, and any ordinary traffic could be carried over that line now. His recent report to me is that it will be practically complete and ready to carry wheat almost in another year. But trains can be run, and the contractors have offered to run a train a week over that line at 25 miles an hour, with safety.

The minister stated about the middle of November that wheat was being hauled over that road. I would like to know to what extent. I put a question on the order paper, and I was told that ten carloads had been hauled. I presume there have been none hauled since.

I gave the answer as received from the engineer. But I think they are not yet doing a regular traffic business on the road. Of course it will only be run

as the contractors run it, and they have offered to put on trains, but I understand there is some difficulty in coming to an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Who is responsible for the insufficient piers and the light superstructure of the Quebec bridge, to which my hon. friend has been making some reference this afternoon? We were told when this scheme was first launched that the government were engaging the very best engineers. They had before them all the construction work of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the weight of rails, the kind of engines that were to be run upon the road, the kind of cars that were to be used, capable of carrying the heaviest freight. But with all that before them, the engineers of the government planned an insufficient bridge. Surely there must have been some great blunder on the part of some person. While I am not going to censure the minister, because he was not in the department at that time, somebody certainly is responsible for that blunder. I think it is fair now that the minister should say who was responsible, so that the country may know where to place the blame.

It might take the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council to decide that question. There was a very long report made, largely technical, in regard to the fall of that bridge. It was planned by a gentleman who was supposed to be the best bridge expert on this continent, if not in the world. There is no question that some one bungled, because the bridge went down. A royal commission investigated it thoroughly, and brought in an exhaustive report, but it is so technical that I would prefer that my hon. friend would read it for himself. It is difficult to say where all the responsibility lies. In engaging an expert so eminent, the government supposed it was protecting itself and the country as well as it could. However, the bridge has fallen down. It-is a great calamity, but it strikes me as a layman that this bridge was beyond the calculations or the principles that any engineers had yet attempted to apply to bridge construction.
Has any of the superstructure that fell down been taken out of the water?

There is a contract let for removing it as far as may be necessary. I think none of it has been removed yet, but they are working at it now. I went out on the fallen bridge or on the debris lying in the water, as far as they would allow me, and the material appeared to me almost perfect as far as the material itself was concerned. The steel was not broken; it was twisted. A gentleman who was with me and who claimed to know something about it, in passing his judgment, said that
the quality of material in the bridge was as good as it could be.
Who was responsible for the lives that were lost?
The Phoenix Bridge Company settled the damages for the loss of life.
Did it cost the government any money?
We have never paid anything in that respect.
No claim against the government?
There has none been made. Occasionally I had some letters, but the Phoenix Bridge Company settled all claims that were made.
But if they settled the claim the government took over all their responsibilities?
We took over the Quebec Bridge Company but not the responsibilities of the Phoenix Bridge Company. The Phoenix Bridge Company were the contractors really.
Are we to understand that for the lives that were lost no responsibility rested upon the government and no money was paid by the government?
Yes.
How much money had the Phoenix Bridge Company been paid by the government?
The Quebec Bridge Company paid them.
But we paid the Quebec Bridge Company.
The Quebec Bridge Company paid them something over $3,000,000 which we afterwards took over as a liability of the Quebec Bridge Company.

I would like to know where the responsibility is ultimately to be found. This, as the minister very truly says, was a gigantic undertaking, therefore, it should have been preceded by precautions as great as were necessary in respect of any such engineering project. But, the situation was this, as far as I understand it, that the government, although practically financing the whole work, left all the contracts to be made by the Quebec Bridge Company, a corporation with a very small capital and utterly unable to proceed with the enterprise without the aid of the country. Eventually the government is obliged to take over the enterprise and in doing so it is sufficiently generous with the people's money to hand back to these gentlemen all

the money they had put into the enterprise together with directors' fees and a ten per cent bonus on the stock.
With interest.

My hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) informs me that I have omitted one item and that I should have included the item of interest which was also allowed to these gentlemen. In the course of these proceedings they had made a contract with some person for the construction of the bridge, and some person must be responsible for the defective , design. The fact that there was a defect in the design, represents, I suppose, $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 to this country, and I think it might be a very legitimate inquiry by the people's representatives in parliament as to whether or not there is some remedy to the people in respect of the undoubted defects which did exist in the design. If the Quebec Bridge Company had proceeded with ordinary business precaution and prudence, they would have had a contract under which some remedy might have been asserted if the design or the execution of the work proved defective, and they should have had that contract with some company which would be responsible in damages to the Quebec Bridge Company and through them to the people of this country for any loss which might be occasioned by reason of a defect either in the design or the carrying out the design. I would like to know exactly what the position is in that regard. I would like to know whether the government have suffered this project to proceed under such conditions that $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 of the public money of this country is represented only by a mass of twisted steel in the bottom of the St. Lawrence river, under such conditions that we have absolutely no remedy at all against any person, or body corporate, or company, for one single dollar of the moneys which had been lost. I think the minister ought to give a very clear and lucid statement of what the situation is in that regard.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has outlined the history of the case pretty accurately. There was in the contract a clause providing for penalties in case of failure, but one regrettable part of it is that it is not so easy to enforce these penalties under the conditions as they exist. The Phoenix Bridge Company is not the original Phoenix Bridge Company that is worth such a large amount of money. The Phoenix Bridge Company is capitalized at $50,000.
Is that paid up? .
I am not sure. It is a limited liability company.
Was it created for the purpose of constructing this bridge?

My own opinion is that it was created for the work of the construction of bridges. It seems to be the practice of these large companies on the other side to organize subsidiary companies for certain work. I admit that when I came to Ottawa, I thought at first blush that we were dealing with the big strong Phoenix Iron Company, which is a rich company, but when I got a little further along I found we were dealing with the Phoenix Bridge Company, which is only a subsidiary company with a capitalization of $50,-OCO.
Was there any security put up by the Quebec Bridge Company to the government for the fulfilment of the contract?

There was a $100,000 bond givep on behalf of the Quebec Bridge Company by a regular corporation. An attempt was made to realize on that bond, but up to date if I am correctly informed it has not been successful. Negotiations are proceeding between the Department of Justice and the company, but the company claim that they were not informed before the expiration of the time when such notice should be given under the terms of the bond.
Who was responsible for the information being given?
It would be the Quebec Bridge Company, I would think.
The $100,000 is lost.

I have not given up all hope of getting it yet. It is in the hands of the Justice Department. We have from the Phoenix Bridge Company a drawback of, I think, $100,000, and there is a lot of scrap metal. I have had for some weeks negotiations through the Justice Department with the Phoenix Bridge Company. But I may say to the committee frankly that, with a capital of $50,000, I have no great hopes that I can collect any great amount of money from the Phoenix Bridge Company, even if we have a case, and, of course, there is always danger in a lawsuit of being thrown out on some technicality.
Is this an American company?

Yes. It is a company that has done splendid work. If I had work of my own to do, and could get security of any fair value from them, I would expect to get as good a quality of work from them as from any other concern on the continent -or any other continent.
That is the Phoenix Iron Company?

The Phoenix Bridge Company, I undersand, has done good

work also. I have recommendations from engineers showing that they have done splendid work.

I think the minister ought to have gone a little further in his description of the way this contract was entered into. He knows that it was entered into with the Quebec Bridge Company, composed of some lawyers and merchants in Quebec who had this charter. They	were	utterly bankrupt as	a	company; but,	just before the end of along session preceding a general election.	they	came forward with	a	contract made with this small Phoenix Bridge Compuny for the construction of a bridge satisfactory to these lawyers and merchants of Quebec. Absolutely no care was	taken	by the government	to	see
that the plans were what they ought to be. The engineer of the Quebec Bridge Company was a very respectable engineer, who had been employed upon the railways of the country, but who, probably, had never been engaged in the construction of a bridge of over two hundred feet-a very respectable gentleman; I know him; but a man utterly inexperienced in this sort of work. In the railway offices they had a very good man on the staff who declined to say that he was responsible for what was done. Within three days of the closing of a long session, the government rushed through an agreement with the Quebec Bridge Company, guiaranteing over $6,000,000 of expenditure that that company had undertaken.
In what year was that?

In 1903, I think. The government brought in a Bill to validate that agreement, land, within the last three days of the session they rushed it through the House of Commons and the Senate, and it became law. The next thing we heard of it particularly was that the bridge was in the river.
It does seem to me that this is the most extraordinary tale of negligence in the management of public affairs that the history of this country can show.
Or any country.

I am perfectly willing to amend it,-this is the most remarkable instance of negligence in the conduct of puiblic affairs that any country has ever known. The mere recital of the circumstances, without any comment at all, is enough to stagger one. The minister has pointed out that this was an undertaking which was almost beyond the limits of engineering skill at that time. The government must have known as well then as they know it now.
I do not think the engineers knew it.

At all events, it was perfectly apparent to the government, the engineers and every one else, that it was a tremendous undertaking. In the first place, they hand over the control and management of that undertaking, they hand over charge of the construction, to a company which practically puts no capital into the enterprise. They exercise no care with respect to the contract; they do not even see that the contract is made with responsible persons or that any adequate security for carrying out the contract is given, by the persons who undertake the work. The work goes on. It is work that requires the very highest order of engineering skill. In the end the whole thing falls into the river. The only thing left for the government to do is to pay off the Quebec Bridge Company, take over their liabilities-not to receive their assets, - because they have no assets of any account-and to proceed with the construction of this work under greater disadvantages than would have affected the undertaking if the Quebec Bridge Company had never intervened at all. The simple statement of the fact that $5,000,000 or $6,000,001) of the money of the people of this country has been spent without any adequate supervision or precaution and is represented solely by the superstructure of this bridge lying at the bottom of the river, with probably no remedy against the Quebec Bridge Company or the Phoenix Bridge Company or any one else, is sufficient without any comment at all. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) is wise in not attempting to make any defence of it. Even he, with all his ability and ingenuity, could not make any defence -no man could make any defence of such a transaction. And it does seem to me that the government, in this particular instance above all others, has shown the most remarkable and unheard of disregard of the public interest and more complete negligence than could possibly have been imagined.

And I would like to bring to the attention of the committee, on this point, the actual figures in connection with this matter. My leader (Mr. R. L. Borden) has referred to the extraordinary negligence of the government as regards proper precautions to see that a proper structure should be erected and proper engineering skill employed-to see, in fact, that such measures were taken as would have prevented this deplorable los3 of money and, worse by far, this deplorable loss of life. In this connection, it might be a little interesting to note for a moment how generous the government is after the event. A month or two ago, I

got the information from the government, and I will give it as it is returned. The total that we have paid to the end of the last financial year in connection with the taking over of this work is $6,424,728, according to the Auditor General's Report. I asked certain questions and the answers were very significant. A large proportion of the money shown to have been spent was utterly unjustifiable expenditure, as I submit. I will read the answer after each question. And I wish, by the way, that the government could arrange to have each answer as it appears in 'Hansard' put immediately after the question to which it relates.
The answer is always given after each question.

I mean that it would be well if they could appear in that wqy. I do not want, in saying this, to get into any quarrel with the 'Hansard' reporters, because they do their work exceedingly well. I asked:
1.	In the total sum of $6,424,718 paid by the government to, or for, the Quebec Bridge and Railway Company during the financial year ending 31st March, 1909, were the following items and sums included and paid, namely:- Interest to the Bank of Montreal on
various amounts advanced to the
company

The answer to that given by Mr. Fielding was very concise: 'Yes'. Then I asked:
2.	What was the rate of interest paid to the bank ?
The answer was:
2.	5 per cent was the rate of interest payable to the Bank of Montreal by the Quebec Bridge Railway Company upon advances made to the company.
The next question was:
3.	Was the interest to be paid by the company to the bank in arrears at the time the government assumed payment of the account?
The answer is: 'Yes', emphasizing the fact that has been referred to frequently, that this was a paper company only, and that when we took over the account we had to pay the arrears of interest which these gentlemen had allowed to accumulate during the time they were nominally building this great national work, and drawing their salaries. I next asked:
4.	Did the bank claim to be entitled to be paid the sum $75,673.18 or any sum, as interest on accrued interest, and did the government pay the sum of $75,673.18, or any sum, to the bank as interest upon accrued interest, or compound interest?

The answer to that is:

Parent received interest, $2,600, and a bonus of 10 per cent on $7,000 capital stock owned by him, and Mr. M. P. Davis received interest, $8,411, and a bonus of 10 per cent on $94,900 capital stock owned by him, in accordance with such agreement.

['Parent received interest, $2,600, and a bonus of 10 per cent on $7,000 capital stock owned by him, and Mr. M. P. Davis received interest, $8,411, and a bonus of 10 per cent on $94,900 capital stock owned by him, in accordance with such agreement.']

I want to say one word more. We paid the interest and bonuses that have been allowed by the government upon the payments into the company by the shareholders. Now, the government, when they allowed that, had the evidence in their hands that the money that was supposed to have been paid into that company by these shareholders was nearly altogether not cash, but direc-

tors' fees for attending meetings. You paid interest on the directors' fees and a bonus, and that was known to the government.
I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to use nickel steel in the superstructure of the new bridge?
I am informed that it is, so far as it is possible to use it, in the compression members and in the principal cords.

The minister has stated that when he came to Ottawa to take his new position as Minister of Railways, he understood that the government had a contract with this strong financial company, the Phoenix, and that if we had any difficulty with that company we would get some redress. My hon. friend has had a very large experience in politics. He was a very prominent member of the Legislature of Ontario and in the government.
Not very long.
That was a matter left in the hands of the electors of the province.
They did not act very well that time.

However, that is another matter. I want to congratulate the government on their ability to put through a scheme of this kind while leading my hon. friend, a very prominent supporter in the province of Ontario, to believe, until he became a member, of the government that they had a contract with this strong company. When he came here and made an investigation he found that the contract was only with a very weak company. With that confession from my hon. friend, surely no one will wonder that the ordinary elector should be deceived. My hon. friend was a student of Dominion as well as provincial politics; he has taken part in all these discussions; and yet it was only after he came here and made investigation that he found that the contract to build this structure, costing many millions of dollars, was given not to a strong company, but to a very weak company. All I can say is that I compliment the government on their ability to deceive the conntry.
My hon. friend was in the House all the time with these documents under his eyes, and he will not take refuge now under the plea that he did not know it was a weak company.
It was like the North Atlantic Trading Company.
I was merely an out sider, an ordinary elector, whereas my hen. fnend was here all the time.
I understand that even the minister did not discover it until after the bridge fell down.
The difficulty is the bridge fell down the night before the hon. gentleman referred to became minister.
Was there any connection between the two events?
Nobody would be sufficiently cruel to say so.
Did the minister say that the_ road between Winnipeg and Lake Superior Junction was not regularly running?
There is no regular traffic over it. The engineers say that the contractor offered to put on a certain service. It 'would have to be run as a contractor's service until taken over.

I want to call attention to what is certainly a grave abuse-the putting of a misrepresentation into the mouth of His Excellency the Governor General in the speech from the Throne. Here is what His Excellency was made to say:
The construction of the Transcontinental railway has made substantial advance during the year. The western division has been extended 66 miles beyond Edmonton, completing a total distance of 861 miles west of Winnipeg. Contracts have been let for 399 miles in the Mountain division; good progress was made on this work. The eastern division is now open for traffic from Winnipeg to Lake Superior Junction and thence, by the Grand Trunk Pacific branch, to the lake itself. The whole of the work between Winnipeg and Moncton is now under contract.
If that conveys any meaning at all, it is an announcement that the road from Winnipeg to Lake Superior Junction is open for traffic, whereas in reality it is not finished or opened for traffic. That was certainly a grave abuse, and the right hon. the Prime Minister went far beyond what he should have done when he made that statement and made the Governor General responsible for it. We have just found out, some three or four months later, that it was simply a piece of deceit.
Has the government a contract for the removal of the scrap from the river, and what is the nature of the contract?
A contract has been let, after asking for tenders, for $45,000, and the debris taken out belongs to the contractor.
He gets $45,000 and the stuff taken out?

Yes

Was the debris in the way of navigation?
Some of it had to be removed on account of navigation and some on account of the construction of new piers.
There are now four piers, two on land and two in the river. Do these occupy the same positions as the old ones?
The south pier occupies the same position, but is enlarged. The main pier on the north side is shifted.
The pier on the south side war partly useful; that on the north side was absolutely useless. What was the cost of the one on the north side?
I have not got that.
Do the two in the river itself occupy the same positions?
I am talking about the two in the river.
Then the two on land, are they in the same position as the old ones?
The two anchor piers have to be taken down.
The old piers then were useless and had to be removed?
They have to be taken down. They will not fit into the new plan.
Part of the bridge did not fall. Will that part be used?
It will have to be taken down. The material may be used for another purpose.
Is the board of engineers to be employed until the completion of the bridge?
Yes, they are engaged, until the bridge is completed, and they are responsible for the engineering department until then. [DOT]	[DOT]
What is their remuneration?	1

$1,000 per month while employed, and a less amount as consulting engineers. During the construction perhaps two may remain as consulting engineers. The engineer who is permanent will, be paid $1,000 a month.

I understood the minister to say there had been a board of three engineers appointed, and the government called in two others to confer with them, and that the whole five had agreed in what should be done.
I do not think I exactly said that.

What will the minister say now, because it is important to know Mr. GRAHAM.
whether there are any differences of opinion?

i My hon. friend, as a practical man, will know that you cannot get two engineers or two architects in the building of a house to absolutely agree on all the details. When the board was appointed, it was provided that should they disagree, they would have the power to call in two other men to confer with them. They have all agreed on the substructure. As to the superstructure, on the great principles they are agreed, but on some details they disagree, and they have the power to call in two other experts to confer with them. If it came to an absolute disagreement, I suppose the majority would rule.
I understood the minister to say the other day that there was practical agreement of the three.
On the substructure there was.
Only on the substructure? Is there disagreement on the bridge itself?

The board are working away. They had differences, these two men were called in, they have given their ideas and the reasons for them. It is likely before they get through that they will absolutely agree on all these things.
They have not agreed yet?
Not on every thing in connection with the superstructure.

It is rumoured in Montreal that there is an absolute disagreement among the three engineers in regard to the superstructure and for that reason these two additional engineers, Mr. Holgate and another, were called in. Is that the case?

If the three had agreed, there would be no need to call in the other two, but they did not agree. I may say frankly it has been no easy task to get along with these three prominent engineers. Of course their reputations depend on their making a success of this bridge. If they make a failure of it, they are ruined professionally. They understand that, they hold very strong views along certain lines, they expressed them strongly and when they first met they were quite a way apart. Each belonged to a particular school, and we have been trying to get the result of the skill of each of them.
I suppose the hon. minister will say that is what the government ought to have done in the first instance.
That is what I am doing.

Why does the minister not have the whole brid.ee constructed of nickel steel? It would be less

work and require no painting. The model modern bridge is the nickel steel one.

I am informed, not altogether. There are certain portions of the bridge in which it is of no advantage to have nickel steel, but where it will be any advantage nickel steel will be used in its construction.
The minister says there is still not absolute harmony on all details. What we understood in Montreal was that a part of the commission wanted a suspension bridge and another part a cantilever bridge.

The difference does not exists there. We arepreparingplans for both. The difference is rather on details of construction which I would not dare to attempt to explain, but I think there will be no difficulty as to disagreements as we proceed.
Have tenders been invited for the superstructure?

Intending tenders have been invited to examine the plans as far as they have gone and to study the plans and specifications for both cantilever and suspension designs. After so many months, in which they will have a chance to study these plans as they go along, we will give them a certain length of time in which to put in their actual tenders.
To whom was the contract for removing the fallen superstructure given?
Charles Koenig, of Quebec.
Are we to understand that there will be no action or responsibility on the part of this government towards the widows and orphans who suffered in this disaster?

I could not say what will happen in the future about any thing. The Phoenix Bridge Company, I understand, assume all responsibility and have settled the claims against them for loss through this great calamity.
Are there any threatened suits against the government?
I have not heard of any.
In looking over the debate I see that the Finance Minister said that this bridge would be ready complete in December, 1906.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was not informed then that it was going to fall.

Neither was the opposition, because we had my hon. friend's statement that the very best engineers would be en-

gaged, the greatest caution would be exercised, my hon. friend would deal with this matter as if dealing with his own affairs. Instead of that we find now that the minister himself says:	Of course the superstructure was altogether too light and insufficient for the work and as for the abutments, they ^have to be added to and strengthened. When we keep in mind the fact that there is no change on the National Transcontinental railway in respect to weight of engines or traffic, we come to the conclusion that my hon. friend and his government blundered and the people of the country are of the same opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If you can conceive of such a transaction as that being my own, I could not have dealt with it in a different way. We had the most eminent bridge engineer on the American continent dealing with the matter, I do not know where a better one could be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
