You had a gentleman from New York, Mr. Cooper, to give advice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Cooper was chosen as the engineer to have direction and charge of the whole work. But there was no question at that time as to his capacity or his eminence.	.

It was proved at the enquiry held in the first instance bv a committee of the House of Commons that when the plans were finally prepared they were sent in for the government's approval, and Mr. Collingwood Schreiber obtained authority from the government to have the plans examined by an American expert. He sought out that American expert, the construction company heard of it, and they protested that they would not allow the work that had been performed in the way of plans and specifications by Mr. Cooper, who^ was their engineer, to be supervised by anybody else. That was abundantly proved in the investigation, and the correspondence is in evidence in both committees of this house. Then the Prime Minister said t,hat if Mr. Cooper had approved of the plans it- would not be necessary to go any further. So there was really no government examination of the plans, and they were approved under those circumstances. Those are the uncontroverted facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not admit they are uncontroverted facts. I regret that I am obliged to speak from memory, to some extent, on a question of-this importance; but my recollection is that Mr. Cooper

was chosen by the bridge company as their engineer, and when it was proposed that there should be another engineer chosen to represent the Department of Railways and Canals, Mr. Cooper objected; and then Mr. Schreiber gave us the advice^ that, inasmuch as the interests of the bridge company and the interests of the government were the same, the opposing interests being those of the construction company, there was nothing to be gained by undertaking to put another engineer there _ as against Mr. Cooper, who was representing the bridge company. But when Mr. Cooper objected to being associated with some other engineer, Mr. Schreiber said: Mt. Cooper is a most eminent engineer, and his interests as representing the bridge company are not at variance with the interests of the government. And I think Mr. Schreiber advised that the matter should be left in Mr. Cooper's hands. I believe the papers will show that to be the fact.

I think my hon. friend is absolutely wrong. It is true that Mr. Cooper was the advising engineer of the bridge company. But who suggested Mr. Cooper to the bridge company? It was the construction company itself, the Phoenix Construction Company. At any rate, the government had nothing else to do, when the plans were sent in for final approbation, than to rely upon those plans after approval by its own engineer. This Mr. Schreiber would not undertake to do. He was called upon to approve of the plans, and he represented to the government that he had not the expert knowledge, the latest expert knowledge as a bridge builder which was necessary to enable him to pass upon so important a matter. When we voted the last sum of money to the bridge company we insisted and the government gave us an assurance, that there would be competent examination by an independent authority. Mr. Schreiber then suggested to the government that he be allowed to employ an expert, and the name of the expert whom he recommended is given in the evidence. Mr. Schreiber had correspondence with that gentleman, who, I think, was from Philadelphia, at any rate he was a man of equal reputation to that of Mr. Cooper. When the company became aware that their plans were going to be examined by an independent authority, they came here and made representations and succeeded in defeating the intentions of the government of having this expert from the United States examine the plans. The Prime Minister himself told Mr. Schreiber, what the Finance Minister has just said, that Mr. Cooper was a perfectly competent man, and if he had found no fault with the plans, then he might affix his signature to those Mr. FIELDING.
plans. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and myself were sitting on that committee, and we obtained from Mr. Holgate, one of the Royal Commissioners w'ho had conducted the first inquiry, the *assurance that the examination by an expert would have allowed them to see what escaped Mr. Cooper, that is to say, a defect in the construction. Mr. Holgate found at once that any independent expert would have detected that defect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend's remarks imply that the government and the company were at variance with the recommendations of their chief engineer, Mr. Schreiber. Am I right in saying that he meant to convey that impression?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then I state unhesitatingly that in that respect my hon. friend is wrong. I say that no step was taken regarding the engineering matters in connection with that enterprise without the cordial approval and support of Mr. Schreiber; and no other engineer was called in to be associated with Mr. Cooper, it was because Mr. Schreiber himself advised that such was not necessary.
Have you got his written advice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am speaking entirely from memory, but I venture to say that Mr. Schreiber will confirm that statement. I was for a short time in the Railway Department, during a portion of the period these negotiations were going on, and I would not have dreamed of taking any step in relation to a work of so great importance, without Mr. Schreiber's advice. I know that Mr. Schreiber was of the opinion that we w'ere getting the best available advice, and that nothing would he gained by insisting on another engineer. I am sure that Mr. Schreiber will say that that is a correct account of what occurred.
It is a question of memory. But I will endeavour to get the absolute proof of what I am saying.
We have been endeavouring to ascertain from the Minister of Railways who was responsible for this blunder.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend might ask who is responsible for any great disaster which occurred. It is easy to find fault afterwards. He might ask who was responsible for the falling of the Tay bridge, who is responsible for the loss of life on the Canadian Pacific railway a few days ago. These things occur in the ordinary way in the management of a great public corporation. Whenever they happen in great corporations little comment is made; but when an accident happens upon

a government work we have 200 odd critics in the House of Commons finding fault which is sometimes unreasonable.
reasonable enough to give the government credit for having taken every precaution in the matter.

I am not trying to hold the government responsible altogether for the accident. But we ou this side have been contending this afternoon that the government were aware that this was a very important work. My hon. friend himself is fully aware that the government was responsible altogether for the payment of money, and for guaranteeing the bonds, because the Finance Minister himself had charge of it in 1903, and came down with a statement in 1904 for the guaranteeing of the bonds. I am not holding the government responsible for the accident. This side of the House has never made any severe criticism of the government on that point. But we are now asking the government, who is responsible for the design of a bridge that was absolutely insufficient for the work for which it was intended? That is the position. It was insufficient, the design was altogether wrong, and that is the reason why this country is put to such enormous expense, and I suppose that is the reason why the bridge fell into the river. As a proof of that we find the government now coming forward and making the statement that the superstructure was altogether insufficient. They have now prepared for a very much stronger and heavier superstructure. 1 would point out to the Minister of Finance that had there been a change in the Grand Trunk Pacific by which larger and heavier engines and trains were to go over this bridge, that would have been one reason why there should be a heavier superstructure. But, there was no change in that respect and therefore, my hon. "friend and his government must be and are held responsible for this accident in so far as that is concerned. The minister can say that the responsibility rests with the engineer if he wishes. That may be his statement, but the people of the country and we of the opposition must seek our redress as against the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I entirely disagree with my hon. friend as to what the people of the country think on this subject. I do not believe that the people of the country expect the members of this government to be engineers. What they do expect is that in a great engineering matter they shall select good professional advice and if it turns out that the engineer made a mistake and if an accident happens on government work, which is just as likely as on any other great work, I suppose that is proof that the eminent engineer was wrong in his judgment. House in Committee of Supply.
Collection of revenue-Intercolonial railway. $9,060,000.
['On Tuesday.']

I wish to say that some hon. gentlemen who were not present this afternoon wish to discuss some items which are covered by the general summary then before the committee, and would like to have an understanding with the minister that this will be open to them. It will not be a matter of detail requiring the presence of the Deputy Minister, but they would like to have left open for further discussion the items of the Intercolonial railway and the Quebec bridge.
I will not object. With regard to this item, hon. gentlemen will notice that we are asking for $250,000 less this year than we asked for last year.

I would like to have an explanation from the minister as to how he has made this reduction-whether it is by cutting down the number of regular hands or otherwise. As a matter of fact, a great many men have been laid off, particularly in the city. of Halifax and its vicinity. I also understand that a number [DOT]of high class men have been engaged at large salaries. I would like to have some idea of how this saving is made.

There has been a general reduction all round. The amount we ask for is based on the experience of the past year; in fact, we think we shall hardly reach an expenditure of $9,000,000 this year, which has been an especially good one for *operation during the winter. Next year, of course, something extraordinary might happen, and we might have a deficit. I will give my hon. friend some items showing how the expenses were cut down last year: steam locomotive repairs, $114,242; passenger car repairs, $1,903; freight car repairs, $114,643; floating equipment repairs, $3,999; shop machinery and tools, $10,566; heating and lighting, $6,493; traffic expenses, $9,637; dispatching trains, $11,882; and various other items of this kind. We did dispense with the services of a large number of men. Quite a number have been taken back, as vacancies occur, and I am asking that the old employees be taken back to fill them.

I quite appreciate, from some personal experience, how impossible it is for the head-of a railway system of some 1,400 miles to put down approximately, as he can do in capital expenditure, what his working expenses will be for the coming twelve months. It is a variable item, and must depend not merely on the number of men employed, and the rate of wages paid, but also on the amount of business done. I desire here to express my great gratification at the departure which has been made by the government from the practice of the past. We have had. year after year, the painful experience of seeing a great public work managed politically. On our side, regardless of whether we should be in power, we desire that this great Canadian institution should be worked for the benefit of Canada, particularly for the benefit of the eastern provinces, regardless of politics. We quite appreciate,
I think, the difficulty of hon. gentlemen opposite in restraining their political friends in the interest of economy, and have tried to make some allowance for that. But there can be no question that so long as a railway like the Intercolonial is worked on political lines, there can be nothing but extravagance and waste. It was for that reason, although I would have liked to have seen the railway removed even farther from the political influence of the government, that I heartily welcomed the appointment of the board of railway men who are now in charge of its operation. I have the more pleasure in saying that much, because in the few months during which these gentlemen have been in charge, we have seen an approach to better things. Year after year, since I have had the honour of being in parliament, I have endeavoured to impress upon the government the absolute necessity of keeping the accounts of this railway as every railway company keeps its accounts-not merely for the purpose of reducing expenses, but for every consideration that applies to any business corporation.
One of the great difficulties we have had in discussing the affairs of the Intercolonial railway has been that we have never been able to compare the results of its operation with those of the operation of other great railways. It has been absolutely impossible for us to take the results of the year's working and compare them with those of any other large concern, for the simple reason that deliberately, wrantonly, , in the face of every experience, the government have insisted upon keeping their accounts on a different basis from that on which other railway companies keep their accounts. If the Intercolonial railway accounts had been kept as are those of the Grand Trunk railway or the Canadian Pacific railway, all the discussions in this

House, which have taken up our time from day to day and from week to week, could have been dispensed with, and the year's operations discussed in two -or three hours. Take such a company as the Grand Trunk railway whose accounts are reviewed 3,000 miles away from here by the men whose money is invested in the enterprise, in a few hours they get at the bottom of the year's work, while it takes us weeks in the case of the Intercolonial railway. Why i's this? It is because the accounts of the Grand Trunk railway and these other.railway companies are kept on a practical system and basis, so that when you find that the working of either of these companies takes a certain percentage of the profits, you have a fair idea whether it is being operated in an economical and businesslike manner. Can we say this of the Intercolonial railway? On that road there has not been any system for charging expenditure as between capital account or working expenses. The system adopted by the government would be laughed to scorn in any business corporation. It is one which conceals the actual results of the work. How can you expect the management to be careful to keep down the expenditure if all the manager has to do is to charge 25 or 30 ot 40 per cent more to capital account and thus show better results? Yet that system has been absolutely fostered, and in fact recommended, by_ the Department of Railways. The minister wants to show a surplus, and it is the easiest thing in the world to do so, if you take 10 or 20 per cent out of the working expenses and transfer that to capital. We can see in the last nine months the beginning of a different system. We find an effort on the part of the management to know precisely what they are doing. For the first time we find these gentlemen setting aside a round sum out of revenue and charging it against the earnings of the road for the purpose of renewing in the future the rolling stock which is wearing out. I would like the minister to show us any such item in the past. These gentlemen have had very little time to show what they can do, but I feel certain that as they go on, further improvement will be shown and, whether the Intercolonial railway shows loss or profit, we shall know the truth. It is absurd for hon. gentlemen from the eastern provinces to tell us from Ontario or elsewhere that we are prejudiced -against the Intercolonial railway. We have no desire whatever to belittle or misrepresent the Intercolonial railway. We do not desire that the Intercolonial railway shall make money unjustly or unfairly to them. We want the road worked honestly; what we want is to know the truth, whether there' be a profit or a loss, and we shall be content.. What more can the people from Nova Beotia or New Brunswick ask? We are not
going to complain if the railway does not make a profit, but we do say that in the interests of honesty and of the country at large, we should know the truth. How can you expect the staff to care whether theyj are doing their best for the railway or not; if it makes no difference whether the rail-' way is really gaining or losing, if they can gain the approval of their employers simply by misrepresenting the actual working expenses of the road? Why, every time you, claim credit in this House by showing a pretended surplus, you hold out temptation to your officers to misrepresent; beJ cause it is very easy for the manager or the engineer or other departmental head, who knows that his reputation in the minister's eyes depends on showing a surplus' -it is very easy for him to show one, and he will take care by every means in his power to do so, especially as he knows that he cannot be subject to criticism, because his accounts are kept differently from those of any other railway management in America. Who in the world can tell whether a railway man has been a success or a failure if his accounts are kept differently from the accounts of every other railway man in America? There can be no greater temptation to wrong-doing on the part of a great staff of employees than to put them in the position they have been in for years. I have -great confidence in railway men. I have had nearly forty years experience of them, and I say there are no men who are more loyal to honest, good working, to the true interests of their employers, than the railway managers: .and officers. The railway man's whole reputation depends upon it. He knows that whatever clap-trap may be uttered on the public political platform, there is a great mass of experienced men over this whole continent who laugh at cooked returns such as we have presented to us. He knows that if he hopes to rise in his career, the worst place he can go to is a concern which keeps its accounts differently from other railways. I am glad this advance has been made. I can see in these, few months' accounts an advance in the right direction.. I do not want to criticise, and it is useless,, in my opinion, to criticise this round sum; set down as the estimtaed amount you may probably have to pay for your working ex-t penses, which, as I have said before, depend upon your traffic. I hope that the minister will be able to go further in the; right course he has taken. 1 hope he wiL>
put the administration of this road more1 and more in the hands of the professional men, as I may call them, who have been bred to the business, and take it more and! more out of the hands of the politicians.

I know my hon. friend will agree with me that it is easier to speak from his standpoint than from the stand-

point of the man who has to do these things. He must have heard some criticism, not unkindly criticism, rather intimating that the appointment of a board was to escape responsibility. I may say that is not my view. I wanted to escape first an enormous amount of detail about which I knew nothing, but which came to my office every day only to be returned to the management and perhaps returned to my office again. I sought, in the first place, a way to get rid of innumerable details and to let them all be settled by men who knew something about that kind of work. However, I am obliged to my hon. friend for his kind words with reference to what I think is an improvement. So far as I am concerned personally, it would be much more comfortable and far easier in one way to continue the old system and have no board. But having undertaken

What way is that?
t Mr. GRAHAM. I will not put that on ' Hansard ' because we never can get it out of there. I am frank in saying and hon. gentlemen will agree with me, that it is a difficult position, a difficult problem to work out. But the board, I think on the whole, has given good results. I am not so anxious to have the Intercolonial railway pay a lot of money, we want to give a good service and the road has been established under conditions that have not allowed it to make much money, but we want to maintain the standard of the road. We want to maintain the service as far as possible, but I do say that at the present time the Intercolonial railway ought to be able to at least pay its own way. It has not any dividend to pay, it has no interest to pay and I think it should be able to support itself. One year we may have a surplus, the next year we may go a little behind.
As to the keeping of the accounts, some three years ago the present deputy minister engaged an expert to go through our books and reorganize the accounts of the Intercolonial railway and get them on the same basis as the books of a company. That cannot be all done in a moment, men who have been working one way all their lives cannot change quickly, but at present our returns are kept on the standard classification of the railways of America. Our reports are made under the head of maintenance of way, maintenance of structure and maintenance of equipment, traffic expenses, transportation expenses, just as returns are made to the Railway Department from all railways operating in Canada. As to charges to capital and revenue we have adopted the standard of the InterState Commerce Commission and whether it be a surplus or a deficit accounts are being kept absolutely as they are kept by a railway company. This year we have Mr. GRAHAM.
charged everything to capital just as a a company would. We have been putting aside $25,000 a month for renewal of equipment since 1907, but not for renewal of rails. This year we are placing $100,000 to one side for rail renewal account and I think that whatever the reports to the House may be they will be shown exactly how the matter stands and will be exactly as the accounts of a company would stand doing the same business.

I am much interested in the remarks of the minister. Whatever may be said, it is certainly a departure, lor many years we have been listening to the predecessors of the Minister of Railways stating to this House that there was absolutely no political patronage in the management of the Intercolonial railway. After the minister had made this statement year after year, he would be endorsed by the hon. gentlemen from eastern Canada emphasizing the fact that whatever other defects there might be in respect to the management of the railway there was no political patronage. We would gather from the_ remarks of my hon. friend, coupled with the fact that they have changed the policy and have now transferred the management to a board, that there had been some political interference. Now the government is being complimented because of the change that has taken place. I want to direct my hon. friend's attention to this remark made in the House a few days ago by a gentleman who lives down in the province where the Intercolonial railway runs, and who is a prominent supporter of my hon. friend's government:
I would like to know if it is in the interest ot the people that the commissioner takes a big stick and threatens a newspaper if it criticises the management that it will get no more patronage, and not only threatens but carries out his threat. That is the way the people's railway is managed for the people. Dod save us from the people's railway.
That is not a criticism by a gentleman from the province of Ontario, that is not a criticism of the old policy, but it is a criticism of the new board of management by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black), showing that there certainly is some interference, that the commissioners do take up the big stick; and if a newspaper down there attempts any criticism of the management of the road, the commissioner says: No more money from the government until you stop that kind of criticism. Now I do not altogether agree with my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). Of course he is a railway man, and his experience is very valuable; but I would hesitate to compliment this new board of management until we see what they are going to do.
I only said I was gratified with what they had done in the way of improvement, but I expected a great deal more.

Improvement in lessening the number of employees. It was charged from this side of the House that they had altogether too many employees on that railway, and we were answered by their saying that, in comparison with other railways in Canada, there were no more employees on the Intercolonial than were required for the passengers and freight. Now we find a number of men have been dismissed. For what reason? Times are prosperous. Surely that is an answer to the criticism on this side. The fact is that a commission appointed by themselves declares there has been altogether too many put on there for political purposes. And now they are dismissed by the railway board, dismissed by the hundreds. A certain great man said that people are bundles of inconsistencies, and I think that remark would apply very well to my hon. friend's department. We have not much to say about my hon. friend, we are waiting until his record is made. My hon. friend from Hamilton thinks he is doing pretty well, but I am not so well acquainted with his achievements. But to-day we have a complete rebuttal from the government side of the policy that they declared was the policy of managing the Intercolonial without any political interference at all. Now I am sorry to have to sit in the House and to find that a criticism, keen and cutting, comes from a gentleman on their own side of the House, who says the management is not a bit better. The commission takes up the stick the same as the government did, and as soon as any criticism comes from a newspaner in eastern Canada about the management-no more support from the government until you stop that sort of criticism.
My hon. friend complains of political interference. He won't feel so badly when he knows that it is a Liberal newspaper that is under discussion.
I was reminding my hon. friend of a criticism of one of his own supporters, and perhaps he would tell us whether that is true or not.
My hon. friend contended that the same political interference was being exercised by the commission as there was before by the minister when they took up the big club.
The hon. member for Hants said that.

No, the hon, member for Hants did not mention political interference. I am pointing out that this cannot be political interference, because it is a Liberal newspaper that is under discussion. As a matter of fact I believe the board did have some disagreement with a newspaper in the east, because the 'board represented to me, and I saw some of the statements myself, that this paper was making a campaign against the Board of Management of the Intercolonial which I have no hesitation in saying was absolutely unfair and based on untruths: and in my private capacity I would not give any business to my best friend if he told what was not true. Of course we have criticism of the Intercolonial management more or less, but no charge of political interference can be made against the board. There would have been political interference if.I had said to the board: 'You must not do that; you must keep on giving this Grit paper business.' But I try to keep my fingers out of the trouble. I hope my hon. friend will see the point.
It certainly could not have been any criticism of a Conservative newspaper, because my hon. friend knows well the Conservative newspapers do not get any pap from the government.

My hon. friend is wrong again, because he does not keep track of things. One of the complaints occasionally made by strong Liberals is that we do give advertisements to Conservative newspapers. That is true. The Halifax ' Herald ' for instance, which the leader of the opposition will recognize, gets advertising; so does the Montreal ' Gazette', so does the Quebec ' Chronicle,' and I could name others, where we get good value. My hon. friend also referred to dismissals. Now, as a matter of fact, the traffic on all roads fell off immensely; every company road, I understand, dismissed their men by the dozens, by the hundred, by the thousand. Wisely or unwisely, I kept our men on. But when the board came in they said there were too many, and they did what a company road would have done a year 'before. I hope that the Intercolonial will get so much business back that we will have to Te-employ some of the men who have been dismissed.
Do I understand that the minister has given the board perfect liberty to advertise in whatever papers they choose, in the eastern provinces or the western, for railway supplies?
For everything in connection with the Intercolonial. The board is doing this now, I could not give you tonight a list of the Liberal or Conservative papers in which they are advertising.

Do I understand
that, so far as the minister is concerned, he gives absolute freedom to the board to advertise in whatever papers they choose?
So far as the Intercolonial! railway is concerned.

There is a certain amount of politics, of course, in connection with the road. But I suppose the minister will not deny that, now when we are two years further away from the general election, the department might exercise some more economy with regard to this $250,000.

This $250,000 is really not in question. The expenditure has been reduced. This year there will be less than the $9,000,000. We took a vote of $9,250,000 last year so as to be sure to cover all contingencies. I am not asking that much now for the experience of last year proves that we will not need it.
. Mr. CROSBY. How many freight passenger cars and locomotives are idle at the present time by reason of the fact that they require repairs? I do not know whether the minister will be able to-night to give me an answer to another question which I desire to ask, but if not I would like him to give it at some other time. I would like to know what the difference is between the number of men getting from $1.25 to $2 a day on the Intercolonial Tailway in 1907-8, and the number of men receiving that wage on the road at the present time. I would also like to know the difference in the number of men getting $2,000 and upwards as between the present year the year 1907-8, together with their salaries.

It would be impossible to get the details that my hon. friend asks for as it would take weeks and weeks to procure the information. In our higher offices we pay our men much less than the railway companies do. [DOT] There has been a good deal of talk to the effect that we pay certain men high salaries and take it out of those receiving smaller pay. The ordinary man on the Intercolonial railway is paid as high, on the average, as men on any railway, or higher, whereas the officials filling the higher offices are paid less than men filling similar positions on other railways in Canada. The criticism of railway men-and we have heard it in connection with the retirement of Mr. Butler from the Railway Department-is that we do not pay sufficiently high salaries to our officers on the railway, and that we do not have enough of these officers. That is the professional criticism on the Intercolonial railway. Just before I came into the department my predecessor took occasion to get the opinion of an expert and his Opinion was as I have expressed it. The criticism is heard that we possibly have too many in the lower grades and too few in the higher, and that while we pay good salaries to the ordinary employees we do not pay our higher officials a sufficient 1 Mr. ARMSTRONG.
amount of money to keep them and to get the best out of them. As to the number of cars, there are about four hundred freight cars ready for repairs and we are turning a greater number out of the repair shops every day than ever before in the history of the road. There are about 5 or 10 per cent of the locomotives ready for repairs, but I find that our percentage of locomotives requiring repairs is less than the average in the Dominion of Canada to a considerable extent. I do not think there are any passenger cars, except those that are always going through the shops.

Last year we had in this House a report from a commission which had been delegated by the government or this House to ascertain whether the clerks in the employ of the Intercolonial railway were getting fairly paid or not.
That was not a commission but a conciliation board agreed to by the men themselves and the management. The House had nothing to do with it.

For the purpose of my argument it does not make any difference. That board went out to ascertain whether the employees on the Intercolonial railway were paid by the standard of other employees on other railways in Canada. They came back with their report, and it was to the effect that they were paid 15 or 20 per cent less.
That was not the report.
Well, what was it?

The report was that we should reduce the staff of clerks and that by this reduction we could pay the balance of the staff a certain percentage of money as recommended by the commission. They recommended that we have a classification something like the Civil Service classification. There were great discrepancies. Some of the clerks were paid too little and others too much, or more than their jobs were worth. We have undertaken to classify these clerks, not by reducing the salary that any person then had, but if a man is getting $1,000 now in an office that under the new classification ought to be worth $750, the old man will retain his classification, but when he goes out his successor will get $750.

That is very good as far as it goes, but I remember when speaking of the matter in the House last session, that a different answer was given to me from that given to-night by the minister. A few days after, when the minister came down with his speech on government railways, he tried to satisfy the House that the Intercolonial railway was run at a

cheaper rate per mile than any other railway in Canada. Then this board went out for the purpose of ascertaining whether the men were overpaid or underpaid, and they reported that there was an over abundance of employees, a matter which was none of their business, because they were not sent out for that purpose. I tried to uphold the minister on that occasion because they were not doing him justice. If they had more men on the road than they should have it was not fair to him. But the minister came in and proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that the railway was not over-manned. I had no reason to doubt the figures which he presented_ to show that that was the actual condition. That being the case, and the management having dismissed as many men as we are informed have been dismissed, we must have a railway which is not sufficiently manned at the present time. I did not have the pleasure of listening to the speech of the hon. Minister of Railways this session, and I have not had an opportunity of reading it, although I hope to do so. Now, I would like to ask the minister what difference there is in the number of men of the working class employed on the Intercolonial railway in 1910-11 as compared with 1907-8, or in 1909-10 as compared with 1908-9. I am sure the minister will be able to give me that information. Then I would be glad if he would give us the information with regard to the number of officials. I understood him to say that the technical men, as he called them, were paid less on this road than on other roads, while the labouring classes were paid as well on the Intercolonial railway as on other roads. No doubt, there are some men on the Intercolonial railway who should not be on the r'oad at all, but if so, that is the fault of the management. .Sneaking particularly of the men in my own locality, including those engaged in connection with the terminal facilities, I do not think they are getting better pay than men who are engaged in other work in that city. In what he said, I suppose, the minister had in mind the fact that his deputy minister has been called to a very high position, at a salary, I believe, three times as much as he was getting here. I want to tell the hon. minister there are not many Butlers in Canada.
Only the first families can have a butler.

I sympathize with the minister in losing his deputy, but we are all pleased that that gentleman has been called to so important a position. If the minister wants to hold his good men, all he has to do is to raise their salaries. Treat the good men well, and do not let them suffer for the bad ones. I suppose the minister
will send me the information as to the number of workingmen on the railway.
I will try to send that to-morrow.

I understand the minister to say that there are about four hundred freight cars of every description now idle. He says also that the number under repair is from five to ten per cent. That is not very definite.

Of course, in our change from the old shop to the new there was some delay of work. But, with the facilities of the new shops, we are effecting a greater quantity of repairs than ever before and are catching up rapidly. I do not take credit for that; it is due to the new shops which were designed and practically constructed by my predecessor.
Prince Edward Island railway, $400,000.
The minister has some explanation to give of this.

I gave that at length the other day. Prince Edward Island is one of the most beautiful spots in Canada. But, so far as railways are concerned, it is isolated. We have a narrow gauge railway there, about 260 miles in length. You cannot give a fair service there and come out even, much less make money. The people of Prince Edward Island have always complained to me- and their complaint is not without Teason -that they do not get the train service they ought to get. They certainly do not begin to get the service that is given on the Intercolonial railway. It is for parliament to look at the matter sympathetically. We must make up our mind that, each year, a certain amount must be contributed out of consolidated fund to maintain the service of the Prince Edward Island railway, for the traffic is not there to keep the road on an even basis financially. But Prince Edward Island is part of the Dominion; the people were brought into confederation expecting great things, and, for my part, I sympathize with the view that we ought to go on and give on that railway a better service than we do now, even though we know that it will increase the amount which must be taken from the consolidated fund.
How much is taken from the consolidated fund for 'this purpose now?

Last year, $90,000; this year it will be about $70,000. We must make up our minds that, if we are going to have the service we ought to have, the service that the rest of us enjoy and would make a fuss if we did not have, it will cost us, say, $100,000. I regard sym-

pathetically the idea that we should give Prince Edward Island a fair service.
Railways and canals-chargeable to capital -canals-Lachine canal - concrete vertical wall, $165,000.

This is for a concrete vertical wall on the south side of the La-chine canal. The slope walls made during the last two years were carried up only to the water line. The portion above water is to be vertical to increase the width of the bank eight feet to twelve feet. Another section of vertical wall is to be built from the top of the rock from the Canadian Pacific railwav bridge to the guard lock, where the dry wall is tumbling down. This wall is similar to the northern wall on the same section. This is a new vote. The items of this expenditure include $22,000 for concrete under water, for the vertical wall $80,000 and for cement about $30,000. Purchases will be made by tender in every instance.
Lachine canal-towards completion of wharf and basins, $135,000.
The tenderers in this case were George Goodwin, the Canadian General Development Company, Downey & O'Brien and Michael Connelly. The contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer.

I would like the minister (Mr. Graham) to notice that when the canal question comes up, he finds that the men of the east are always prepared to see that the money necessary is provided. All they ask is that that money shall be properly spent. The men from the east are anxious to have every facility provided for the transportation of the commerce of this Dominion. So, I am glad to say, you do not find them trying to interfere with these estimates in any way.
Were tenders asked for in all the cases the minister has mentioned?
Yes.
By advertisement in the newspapers?
Yes. Formerly, we sent circulars to the cement manufacturers, but now we advertise in the papers for cement also.

I do not wish to criticise too closely on this point, but we ought to understand the policy of the department. Are we to understand that advertisements are given to the newspapers having the largest circulation regardless of party. Or what is the policy of the department on that point?

So long as men are human there will be humanity in all these Mr. GRAHAM.
things, I suppose. The policy of my department, in regard to large works like the Quebec bridge, is to advertise in all the trade papers and engineering papers, which will reach particularly the men who would be able to undertake the work. General work we advertise in papers of good repute, and I am free to confess that they are mostly Liberal papers.

For instance, looking over the list of papers in Toronto, I find in connection with one item that $228.60 was paid to the Toronto ' Globe ' and $228.60 to the Toronto ' Star ' * but I look in vain for any advertisement given to any other of the leading papers in Toronto.

Upon the basis of my hon. friend's suggestion, it is said by those who know that the Toronto ' Globe ' has the largest circulation, inside and outside, of all the Toronto papers. It is said that the ' Star ' has the largest circulation of the evening papers. So that outside of politics these would be the two papers that would reach the most people.
Accepting my hon. friend's policy of selecting the papers having the largest circulation-
I did not say that.

There can be no other inference from his statement that the Toronto ' Globe ' has the largest circulation of the Toronto papers and the ' Star ' has the largest evening circulation. Keeping that in view, I want to direct his attention to the fact that when advertising is done in the city of London, in western Ontario, my hon. friend does not select the paper there having the largest. circulation, because in the London ' Free l'ress ', which is recognized as the leading newspaper in that section, you cannot find any government advertisements.	Therefore, the policy
which my hon. friend has laid down applies to the city of Toronto, but not to the western part of the province. I am not complaining particularly. I merely want know exactly what the policy of my hon. friend is.	My hon. friend says,
therefore we may expect that in the future advertisements will appear only in papers that support my hon. friend and his government, and therefore the patronage list, which we have heard so much about lately, is not going to disappear altogether from the government, even from my hon. friend's department.

I may be blunt, but I am not hypocritical. As long as I find a friend who gives me good service, I am inclined to lean a little towards that friend, and I am inclined to think that my hon. friend would do the same.

I am very glad to hear that that is the minister's policy, because it means that he will do all his advertising in the Halifax 'Herald' and 'Evening Mail,' which I think have the largest circulation east of Montreal, if not in the whole Dominion. They are also perfectly independent. No man can have their support unless he is worthy of the support of the people. Therefore, these papers, having been brought to his notice, being perfectly independent, and having a sworn circulation, I hope that the minister, whenever he wants to let the people know what he wants, will advertise in them.
How much will this item cost altogether?
What is the cost of the other item?

It is expected that the vote will cover the entire cost; but we have not yet let the work.
Soulanges canal-purchase of tool grinder, &c., $850.
How are articles of this kind bought?
All \>y tender. I have a list of 300 of the leading machinery men, irrespective of politics, and I write to all of them for tenders. It is cheaper than advertising.
What we have had to complain of is that the government bought through middlemen.

We do not buy any tools from middlemen, unless they are recognized agents of their respective companies. In every case we try to buy direct from the manufacturer. In fact, in some cases I have told the manufacturer that he must tender direct.

I believe that the minister means what he says, but in the Mer-win case we found that the manufacturer was willing to sell and deliver at his price to the middlemen, but the government bought in preference from the middleman and paid him 87 per cent extra..

There is nothing of that kind in my department.
Soulanges canal-stopping leaks, trimming slopes, &o., $100,000.

Last year we asked for $160,000 and spent $60,000. The Soulanges canal is built through soft soil, which is very treacherous, and we are trying to improve the banks so that it will be impossible for us to experience the trouble we had in the Cornwall canal. The work we have done has proved very efficacious, the bank being dry where it used to be wet and
spongy. We are completing that work, which must be done in the interest of shipping.
Will that cover all the work to be done?

It will cover this particular work and overcome what appears to show signs of difficulty. We have to take the responsibility of keeping up the work to prevent any recurrence of this kind.
Sault Ste. Marie canal construction, $70,000.

This work is under contract. It is for deepening and widening the channel at the upper entrance. We let this by tender to C. S. Boone, of Toronto, who made the lowest bid. Contract dated 12th March, 1907, value of work done to October last, $200,380. We hope that this $70,000 will complete the work.
Trent canal construction, $1,750,000.

Last year we had a million dollars. This year we expect to let two more sections, which will bring us from Lake Sirncoe to Lake Ontario. We expect to have all that under contract this year. My trip through the various canals in the old world convinced me that the Trent canal will be of real advantage to the Dominion. Quite a lot of water-powers will be developed along the way, and the dams constructed by us will assist in the development of more power. We have made arrangements with people who own the land along the banks wherever we could, and we expect that there will be developed altogether in that part of the province some 60,000 horse-power. Some two years ago, in order that the rates might be right, I amended the Act of the Board of Railway Commissioners and placed the rate to be charged by the people who develop these powers under the control of the board.
How much still remains to be done after these contracts are completed?

From Simcoe to Georgian bay, there is one route by Nottawasaga bay and the other by the Severn river. I expect to meet a deputation concerning these routes in a few days. One part of the people desire the canal to go by Nottawasaga, and the other by Orillia, taking the Severn river.
It will be of no use for the craft that sail on the upper lakes?

No, it will be for canal barges drawing eight to nine feet of water. I look to a good deal of development of traffic that will come through in these barges. The opening of this canal will make that part of Ontario one of the paradises of Canada for summer tourists.
How many locks? And is there any estimate of the cost of the work?

The engineer has not yet finished his report as to these two routes, the Severn river and the Nottawasaga. My hon. friend from Simeoe (Mr. Currie) looked over part of the report in my office. I do not know whether it pleased him or not. My hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright) was looking at it to. The report will be completed and give a full estimate of all my hon. friend asks.
The Newmarket canal no doubt will get its full share.
My hon. friend from York (Mr. Wallace) is waiting for that.
What is the hon. gentleman appropriating for the Newmarket canal?

Last year we did not spend much on it. I sent for Mr. Grant, the engineer of the department, who is a first-class man, and we discussed the Newmarket canal very thoroughly. He assured me that I can state to the House on his reputation that there will be plenty of water in that canal. Before the summer is over, you will find that the stretch then completed will have water in it.
It has none now.

Yes, they are skating on_ it. I am giving you what my engineer says. This year we intend to spend about $150,000 on that portion of the Holland river canal. Of course that is the portion in the vicinity of Newmarket. There is another section east of that called No. 2, Holland river, which requires dredging, but we have not done anything on that yet.
Last year you spent about $192,000.
$57,000, I think.
You were to have spent the same as the year before.

I did not do it.
Mr. WALLACE, The year before most of the money was spent during August, September and October, 1908. That is the reason I thought this work was mostly political. Does the minister really intend finishing that canal, and has he any idea that it will be of any use whatever
I do intend finishing it.
And you will get water?
Not the faintest question about it.
Where do you expect to get it?

I am giving Mr. Grant's opinion. In Germany last year I visited one canal owned by a county council. The canal was 26 miles long, and it was supplied entirely from the drainage of the country. In Germany last year I visited one canal 29 miles long supplied absolutely by the drainage of the country. It joined a river, but the county council was precluded from taking any water from the river because a rival company had the monopoly of the water from the river. They made provision that in case the water supply ran low they can pump the water back into the canal and use it again. They have a system of double locks by which a boat goes through on one side and the same water is used for another boat on the other side of the canal. They have never used the pumping device as they get enough water from the drainage. It is one of the most beautiful places in Germany, and is a fashionable summer resort. Mr. Grant says that by a system, I think, of two dams and reservoirs they can provide ample water, and after-discussing it with him 1 have not a lingering doubt in my mind that there will be plenty of water for the Newmarket canal.
What is the estimated cost of the canal with the water? Last year you said $982,000 w'ithout the water.
Unlike my hon. friend, I always include water when I give an estimate for a canal. The estimate will be as I said last year, at least $1,000,000 in my opinion.
When do you expect to have the canal finished?
If my hon. friend is in a hurry, I can spend some more money.

I do not think you should spend any.
Mr, GRAHAM. I have taken that we should not construct more branches until we finish the main work. When existing contracts have been completed, I intend to stop toying with this project and go on and complete it. This year I intend to spend $150,000 on it.
Has the government come to a conclusion as to the best means for irrigating the Newmarket canal?

I could understand the necessity for a canal where water had to be pumped in and out if after-having it in the shape there would be any traffic. I know that vicinity and I know that there is very little water to be got to go into that canal. I would make a special appeal to the minister to stop spending money on a useless work like that. I am appealing to the minister as a business man on a business proposition even in the

face of the report of the chief engineer. If the minister would go there himself and look into the proposition and come back and tell us that he thinks it is feasible to keeri that canal supplied with water, and that when completed there would be an}' business or traffic, I would be willing to put up some money. You should stop building this canal, it is a work which should not go on because there are so many necessary works all over the country that are not being gone on with. I am satisfied that the minister feels he should not go on with it, but something is compelling him to make the expenditure. I am sure that if he had his own way he would not do it.

If the hon. member had been in Ottawa some years ago and had had the privilege, which was my privilege of listening to a very large and representative delegation from that section of the country, headed by Mr. Lennox, a member of the legislative assembly of Ontario, I am sure his faith in the Newmarket canal would have been strengthened, and he would have been convinced beyond all question that it was a work in the interest of Canada, as well as in the interest of that section of the country, that there was abundance of water, that traffic was there waiting only to be carried, and that unless this parliament acceded to the very reasonable request of these gentlemen, parliament would be doing an outrage on the people of that section and on the people of Ontario generally. I was impressed by the earnestness of the appeal made and the representation with respect to the project.
Did not the minister make any investigation?
There was a very thorough investigation.
What amount of traffic was stated to be likely to go through the canal?

I cannot recall now, but it was a number of years ago, and I am speaking of the impression made on my mind as to that. It was said that this traffic would mean a traffic to the city of Toronto as well as the country near the canal.
What class of goods was it expected would be carried?

Very largely lumber and materials that were to be brought down from the central point there in Haliburton through Lake Simcoe, through the Kirk-field lock, and on towards Aurora, and thence carried to Toronto. It was said that the manufacturing interests of Toronto would be largely advantaged, and that the resources surrounding these interior lakes would be given life, and the
people of that section of the country would' reap the benefits which are denied them today by reason of the lack of transportation.
Did you, ever see the feeder where the water is to go through for the Newmarket portion?
I have never personally seen it.
Does he remember the first estimate that the deputation asked the government for?
I do not carry it in my memory.

That deputation did not ask the government to build a canal from Lake Simcoe to Newmarket, but for a small appropriation to deepen the Holland river from Lake Simcoe to Holland Landing. In former day3 boats used to go from Lake Simcoe to Holland Landing. The chief reason why the Prime Minister and the Minister of justice justified that canal was that a deputation came down from North York, and there happened to be three or four Conservatives among them. Well, if that circumstance is a sufficient reason for this government to spend $1,000,000 on that canal, I am not able to see it myself. The deputation asked for a small expenditure, and the premier said that because Mr. Lennox was on the deputation, who he supposed was a member of the local House, that justified him in spending a million dollars. But I would remind the committee that the deputation did not ask for any such thing, they only asked for about $100,000. just enough to deepen the canal. It was Sir William Mulock who brought that deputation down here; he invited a few of his friends to come down to Ottawa. You can get any number of people to come down here on a little trip like that.
That was his own county.

Sir William Mulock was the representative of North York at that time, and he got this deputation to come down here. It was a little pleasure jaunt for the purpose of seeing the capital. But that is the reason the government gave for spending a million dollars there. That is the minister's estimate here to-night, but I am sure that by the time they get through with it it will cost $2,000,000. Before that time there had not been a dollar spent on that canal, except in survey work, according to figures brought down by the Minister of Railways last year. I do not think it is fair to try to make the country believe that Mr. Lennox, because he happened to be the local Conservative member, would come down here and ask the government to spend $1,000,000 on a useless work like that. The ex-Minister of Railways 3ays he

does not remember what the first cost of that was. But all they asked for was a small sum of money, which has now grown to $1,000,000, and will probably be $2,000,000 before they get through.

I happened to be Minister of Railways at the time this_delega-tion came. I cannot speak as to the politics of those gentlemen, but I remember that the delegation was headed by Mr. Lennox. I assumed that they came as business men, and not as politicians, and I did not treat with them as politicians, but as a representative delegation from that section of the country, coming here for the purpose of impressing upon the government the necessity of this work. I remember that they emphasized the fact, they claimed it to be a fact, that it would be a very easy matter to clear out the Holland river to Holland Landing, which they said was the old route to the Georgian bay, and they only required a comparatively small sum of money to build that portion of the work. But they laid stress upon the necessity of extending that work up from Holland Landing to the interior, to Newmarket.
Clear through to Aurora.

Yes, that far. Now, I am sure this delegation were in earnest. Subsequently I had the matter inquired into by an engineer, one who was not connected with the department at that time, and he made a report with regard to the estimated cost, and the traffic as well. I cannot carry in my memory, of course, what the report was. It is true that the then Postmaster General, who represented that constituency, took a deep interest in the work, and he and the local representative in the Ontario legislature seemed to be united in an effort to secure the construction of this work for that section of the country.
Perhaps the hon. member for Westmorland could tell us whether any estimate was made by the department in his time of the probable traffic that would be carried over this canal?

I cannot give any details, and I only speak from memory as to the importance of the traffic, and from their representations. They convinced me, at least, that a traffic would come from the section to which I have referred, from the lakes away up to the Haliburton country, and from the Black river, and from the Georgian bay. They represented that material would be brought from the shores of the Georgian bay through the Trent Valley canal to Lake Couchiching, and from Lake Couchiching to Lake Simeoe, thence into Aurora, and thence on to Toronto.
Then the hon. member himself is practically responsible for the canal being started?

I certainly am, and I take all the responsibility that belongs to me. There is one thing I am always ready to do, I am always disposed to lend a listening ear to the people, to gentlemen coming here on the part of the people, seeking the people's interest, and I have yet to be convinced that it was not in the interest of the people to begin that work.

Year by year we are told by the government that this Newmarket canal was built in response to the request of a deputation that accompanied Sir William Mulock and Mr. Lennox, who at that time, or subsequentliy, became the local member for that county.
He was at that time.
Perhaps the hon. member could tell us what year that was in, so that we may know whether he was the local member at that time.
He was introduced to me as the local member for that constituency in the Ontario legislature.

I infer from what the ex-Minister of Railways has said to-night, that the object of that deputation was not to get a grant of money to construct this canal. What these people wanted at that time was something different, a sum, as he has told us, for deepening the Holland river, which would be a small part of this canal, and would cost but very little money.

I do not wish my hon. friend to be under any misapprehension as to what I stated. I said that they had spoken of the deepening of the Holland river as far as Holland Landing as a work that would not be very expensive. They emphasized the fact that it would not cost very much to do that, but that the important work and that which they sought, urged and solicited was the extension of that canal to Newmarket and Aurora.

What I have heard in the discussions in this House in reference to the whole matter was that the deputation did not have in their minds the extension of the work which the government is at the present time undertaking. I do not think it ever entered into the minds of the people who came down at that time that the work was to spread out into a section of country where no water could be found for canal purposes, where practically no traffic sufficient to warrant the expenditure could- be obtained. I am still under the impression it was only the small part that the people at that time asked for, namely the deepening of the Holland river.

I do not think that the ex-minister will succeed in convincing this committee that the larger project was ever thought of by that deputation. I have never been able to accustom myself to the idea that that was the real intention, nor can I imagine that the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals was so extremely liberal, even to help the few Conservatives wno accompanied that deputation, that he would at once jump into an expenditure that was going to amount anywhere from $1,000,000 to $1,500,000. I do not think it ever entered into his mind that he was going to do that. I do not think he ever contemplated anything of the kind. I do not think that he ever asked this House for an initial appropriation that was going to spread out to such a large sum. I think we might as well drop the idea that when the matter was initiated in the first place by the deputation which came down from the northern part of the county of York, headed by Sir William Mulock and Mr. Lennox, the local member, they ever had in contemplation any such outrageous expenditure. The ex-minister, I think, must see by this time that he made a mistake in venturing on such a broad scheme with the limited information he had. I confess that this is the talk all over that part of the country. It is the wonder of the people who go to see the Newmarket canal. They laugh at the idea. It is simply a matter of ridicule and no one who looks at the work ever thinks of justifying the government in this annual expenditure that is going on. I would appeal to the minister, as other hon. members have done, just to drop this matter of the Newmarket canal. Enough money has been spent on it. I do not think the country will lose anything if we just sink what has been spent and pay no more attention to the undertaking. Now, I have one question to submit to the minister. He informed us a short time ago that the engineer had assured him of the possibility of securing water for the canal.
I said the probability- the surety-not the possibility.
Possibility.
No not the possibility.
The absolute certainty?
Yes.
Is that strong enough?
Yes. That is his opinion.
There is no doubt that you can make anything absolutely certain if you spend enough money-almost anything; I will not say anything.
There are some limitations.

I do not doubt that
if the minister puts pumps at work some where about Lake Simcoe he can provide enough water to fill this canal. That would be an absolute certainty, but what I want to know is whether the engineer gave him any estimate as to the possible annual cost of keeping this canal filled, and, if so, what that estimate is. How much are we to vote year after year for the purpose of supplying water for this canal? Will it be $50,000; will it be $100,000? Would it not be cheaper for this government to hire ox teams and convey the traffic over this route along which it is expected to build this canal than to expend money for the purpose of supplying water for the canal? I would like to know if the minister has any estimate of what it will cost yearly to supply water?

I cannot permit my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) to take his seat without making one statement. I have made the statement that this delegation came here, that it did not come here as a political delegation, as far as I recognized it at least, and that it pressed upon the department and myself as representing the department the absolute necessity, in the interest of that section of the country, of not only deepening the water-way of the Holland river as far as Holland Landing, but of extending the canal to Newmarket and Aurora. I have made that statement in the presence of my hon. friend. If, personally he cannot believe it, under the rules of the House he is constrained to say that he must accept it. These are the facts. It is not a matter of any moment to me now. I am speaking of it as an occurrence that transpired. I have a very distinct recollection of the circumstances of the delegation. I was impressed, in the first place, by the size of the delegation. We are not accustomed to have, in our eastern country, very large delegations. They usually send two or three men as spokesmen on behalf of a section of country. There is a different custom pursued in Ontario. I remember being assailed by a good many delegations not assailed, but I had the honour of meeting a very large number-I remember, in connection with the Trent Valley water-ways. I had great faith in the advantage that is to accrue to Ontario in connection with the Trent Valley water-ways, and that faith was strengthened by a close study of the conditions in that section of the country and by going over the route. Now, in connection with that, I looked upon the extension of the water of Lake Simcoe, up through the Holland river and on to these other points, as a work that was incidental to the comple-



tion of the Trent Valley water-ways. If there is not that traffic for the canal, if there is not that wealth of resource that was represented, so much the worse for that section of the country, but it seems to me that if the Trent Valley water-way is of any advantage to the interior of Ontario, if it is any advantage to the city of Toronto, and to the cities, towns and industrial centres along the shores of Lake Ontario to secure the development of the resources in that region, surely as a preliminary condition it is necessary not only to complete the Trent Valley canal, but it is as well a necessity to extend this canal up through the Holland river and beyond.

I am not sure that there is very much difference between the ex-Minister of Railways (Mt. Emmerson) and myself touching this question. What I said, or intended to say, was that the primary object of that deputation was to secure the deepening of the Holland river.
That would be a necessary incident of the extension of the canal.

I never understood that the deputation at that time contemplated the large expansion of work that has since been proposed. And I cannot think that the ex-Minister of Railways would have entertained the proposition at that time if he had thought that it was going to expand so as to call for an expenditure of a million or a million and a half. The ex-minister adheres to the point that he understood that their primary object was the deepening of the Holland river, but that they did make reference to the expansion of the work.
That they pressed it.

But I have always understood that what they were in search of was, mainly, money for the. deepening of the Holland river, not that they expected the minister to extend the work all over the country and involving such vast expenditure.
They only limited it to Newmarket and Aurora.

It is a matter of memory; it is unwritten history; but the people in that section have the impression that the work, whether undertaken in response to that deputation or for any other reason, is a work that is absolutely useless, that it is unworthy the expenditure that the minister is asking to make upon it. I simply give my understanding of it. I am not going to dispute the ex-minister's memory in the matter. I take my information from general inferences and Mr. EMMERSON.
what I think to be reasonable conclusions. Now, I would like to know from the minister how much it is going to cost yearly to supply this canal with water.

The county of York is a very advanced county, so I suppose that when the hon. member (Mr. Henderson) speaks of ox-teams, he speaks metaphorically. Water for this canal will be supplied as water is supplied for other canals, by storing water naturally flowing on the watershed. The engineer tells me that the location is excellent and that the construction of one or two dams will have the effect of maintaing a fair water supply. As to the traffic, if we had stopped to discuss the traffic along any part of the Trent canal, and be guided in our determination by the traffic in sight, we should never have constructed any part of that canal. The probability is that, had a similar test been applied, the Rideau canal would never have been built. Had the traffic in sight only been discussed, many railways would never have been constructed. Certainly, had the authorities of Ontario stopped to discuss the traffic in sight in the north country, there would have been no Toronto and Northern Ontario railway. The question of traffic is always problematical, but these lines of transportation do seem to develop traffic for themselves.
That is a rather comprehensive rule that the minister lays down-that in deciding upon the construction of a canal you do not need to consider either the cost or the traffic.
I did not say that.
But what the minister did say amounts to about that. Would he be good enough to say how much of this vote represents work on the Newmarket canal to be done during the coming year?
I think that we expect to spend $150,000.

This is a proposition that every person who goes near it knows is utterly unworthy of completion. I am sorry that the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) has stated that he is practically responsible for it. He has told us that Mr. Lennox and others came down here and made certain representations. It seems to me that it was his duty at that time to find out more about this matter than he did. I do not like to say anything unkind at any time, but I canhot but feel that, if he was to be so easily imposed on as this, we need not be surprised that he lost his job. Anybody knows that, in order to get water into a canal, unless you depend upon the rain, you must have some

feeders. I would ask the ex-minister and the minister also what lake there is to feed this canal; and, if there is no lake, where can the water come from except by pumping it back from Lake Simcoe?

And I would remind the minister (Mr. Graham) before he speaks that my question was: How much will it cost annually to provide the water for this^ canal? I am not asking simply how it is to be done. The minister used a great many words, beat about the bush, and told us about their plan to have reservoirs, and about the practicability of that plan; but he evaded the point as to how much it is going to cost. Are we going to get value for the money we are to spend?

I have tried to make it clear to my hon. friend, but I am afraid he ia bound that he will not understand. He suggested that I said that we would have to pump the water, and he wanted to know how much it would cost to get the pumps. 1 told him that the water for the Newmarket canal would be supplied in the same way as water for all canals where rivers are united, by a system of storage dams and reservoirs; and my engineer tells me that there is not the slightest doubt that there will be plenty of water if it is properly stored. That is on the word of one of the best engineers we have in the service jn regard to hydraulics, and a most reliable man, and I think his assurance is worth more than my private opinion or that of any one else on that point.
An engineer, Mr. Walsh, made a report before this work started, as to the ample water facilities for the canal.

It seems as if the minister has gone to Germany to gather information to enable him to come back and spend more money on the Newmarket canal. I would like to ask him whether, in sending his engineer to investigate the water supply of the canal, he instructed him also to investigate the amount of traffic that would likely be on that canal after it was completed?

I have made the statement in a general way as to the traffic. I did not send an engineer to report on the canal. The engineer to whom I refer was the resident engineer of the Trent canal system, who has had charge of all the dams and reservoirs which have been constructed, and he says that with storage provided there will be ample water for the Newmarket canal. He has made no mistake on anv other part of the Trent canal system with regard to storage, and I have not the slightest doubt that he is perfectly correct as to this.

The present statement of the minister is most indefinite and unsatisfactory, and must bring us to the conclusion that we should vote directly against this amount of money being passed at the present time. If the minister will go into that country and investigate for himself, I am sure that he will come to the conclusion which I came to long ago. I was bom within 30 miles of Newmarket, and know that country thoroughly, and there is no way possible to get water for that canal except to build large dams and reservoirs to hold the water, or else to pump the water up. And when the canal is built, how much traffic will it get from that district? The ex-Minister of Railways told us it was a timbered country. If he went there, he would find that it is the very opposite. I plead with the minister, that before he spends another million dollars on this useless work, which will have no traffic worth speaking of and little or no water, he should make use of the money in another direction. It was only last fall that I had the opportunity of looking at the canal that was being built, and I cannot too strongly condemn the expenditure of such a large amount of money for such a useless purpose.

I think it must be evident to every man of this committee that this project was undertaken without going carefully into the matter and obtaining such information as would warrant an undertaking of this kind. There does not appear to be any person here ready to defend it. We can hardly dignify with the name of defence the statements put forward by the minister this evening. I would suggest to, the minister that instead of asking the House to vote this money for this purpose, he take a portion of it and expend it on a canal that will give tangible results, namely, the Wolfe Island canal. Let him deepen that canal, whidh will shorten the distance between Kingston and Cape Vincent by between 15 and 20 miles; and I can assure him that he will have any amount of water for that canal, as long as Lake Ontario remains as it is.

I wish again to enter my vigorous protest against this expenditure on the Newmarket canal. The minister has associated this work in some manner with the Trent Valley canal system. It does not seem to me to be the part of wisdom to open up doubtful tributaries for the Trent canal when you have no outlet for that 'canal at either end. In building a railway, you build the main line before the branches; and it seems to me that the same principle should apply to a canal. The first thing to do with the Trent Valley canal, if it is ever to be made effective, is to complete it through to the Georgian bay. In that way it might be made of some benefit to the

people of Canada, in affording an outlet for the grain delivered at Midland and other ports on Georgian bay. With regard to the deputation that came to the ex-minister, as the name of Mr. Lennox, the local member, has been mentioned in connection with it, I want to say that I interviewed him with regard to this matter not many months ago, and he emphatically informed me that when that deputation was arranged for, and he was invited to join it, it was only intended to ask the government to deepen the Holland river. The building of the Newmarket canal was an after consideration and no part of the original scheme; Sind if some members of the deputation undertook to enlarge it when they came here, they got up the deputation under false pretenses, and got men to come down in support of a scheme that.was not placed fully before them before they left home. A great deal has been said with regard to the water supply of this canal; but no water will be needed, because no vessels will ply up or down that canal. It will do as well dry as wet. So I do not see that we need trouble ourselves with the question of water for the Newmarket canal. They may cut it up and make pig pens out of it for the farmers when completed, but otherwise I do not think it will be of any value to the people. However I do not want to bother about that phase of the question. The minister ought first to open up the Trent Valley canal, and then, if he has money to waste, take up the Newmarket canal.
