That is hardly fair. We did not vote it down. An amendment was moved that the vacancy should be filled by a man having a knowledge of railway conditions in the west. The original motion was to appoint a farmer. We changed that because we did not want to confine the appointment to one particular class, but to be enabled to get a good man from any class.

The resolution from this side asked for the appointment of a farmer. My hon. friend differed from that and had an amendment moved from his side of the House, and the first resolution was voted down. The first resolution was to the effect that as a farmer occupied the position, Mr. Greenway, the government ought to put a prominent farmer from the west in his place; and to assist the government, this side of the House moved the resolution.
Are you sure that was the reason ?

Well, the government had been making such professions on behalf of the farmers throughout the west that we thought we would point out that, so far as our side was concerned, we were favourable to the farmers. But my hon. friend differed from us and had the motion amended. When may we expect the appointment to be made?

I would not like to name the day. I have my own views as to the wofk of the commission. My opinion is that we ought to have a man from the west, and when the vacancy is filled, it will be by a western man.
Will he be a farmer?

Not necessarily, but we will take a good man, no matter what his calling may be. I have had very prominent farmers there recommending a professional man, and giving reasons why it would not be wise to appoint a farmer.
Perhaps the minister is waiting for the photograph oi the Calgary applicant.
Will the Minister of Agriculture tell us whether ne has urged on the Minister of Railways the necessity of appointing a farmer or whether he intends doing so?
I voted for the resolution that passed the House.
The Minister of Agriculture recorded bis vote against the farmer.
No.
He voted for the amendment of the government.
Hear, hear.

And the original resolution was that the government should appoint a farmer. That did not suit the Minister of Agriculture. He said we must not bind ourselves to appointing a farmer and he voted to enable the government to appoint another man. He will not say that, in that respect, he was very enthusiastic for the farmers.
I am always enthusiastic for the farmers.

The Minister of Agriculture was out west last summer among the farmers and he must have handpicked a number of them and selected one he could recommend to his colleagues. I am surprised that the Minister of Railways should still adhere to the position taken by that side, that the new commissioner must not be a farmer.
I did not take that position.
And unfortunately a relative of the minister seems to be a favourite in the west for the position, and the minister is blocked from appointing him by last session's resolution.

I think that professional men are well represented on the Board of Railway Commissioners, and that it is due to the farmers that they should have a representative on that board. I do not think that the minister could do better than appoint a farmer thoroughly acquainted with the conditions out west, and I would strongly urge him to do so.

I wish to press the view of my hon. friend who has just sat down. I think the board is well filled with professional men, and there is no class o.f peonle who do more for the country than the farmers. They are well entitled to representation on the board, and I am satisfied that the minister can find many able farmers in the west who could fill the vacancy very successfully.

I think we are entitled to some expression of opinion from the Minister of Agriculture. He will no doubt be going around the country next summer saying that this matter was not drawn to his attention. We wish to give him the opportunity of saying whether he still believes a farmer should be appointed. Has he made any recommendations to the minister on behalf of an}' farmer for that position?
No.

There are so few positions to which farmers can be appointed that I think we should leave them this one. Everything else in the service is blocked out for professional men, so that when a farmer makes application he is met with the statement you are not a graduate of any university and you have not professional training, &c. I really think that, in all fairness, as a matter of justice to the farming community, especially in the west, who have such vital interests at stake, the minister should be frank enough to tell the House that, all other conditions being equal, a fanner will be given the preference for this position.
Remuneration to government directors, Grand Trunk Pacific, $2,000.
I would like to ask a question. Are the officials of the Railway Commission allowed transportation under the Railway Act like members of parliament? It is vitally important they should be, if not.

I think they are provided for in some way. I know they do get transportation. I will look into that. I think they are included in the class that the statute provides the railway shall carry free.
Mr. ,T. A. CURRIE. The reason I ask is that it is rumored that such is not the case, and it, would be very unfortunate if it were not.

I shall make a note of it. I see the distinction.
To pay expenses in connection with cases before the Railway Commission, $10,000.

We spent last year $5,470.77. We have cases come up in which the department is interested, and we sometimes initiate cases on behalf of the government. Take, for instance, the express investigation.
Railways and canals-collection of revenue -canals-statistical officers, $37,506.
I hone the minister will look up some of the statistical records. He will find they are borrowed mostly from American publications.
We get all our own original returns and abstract the American returns as well.
How many officers are permanently employed?
On the canals, all told, about 3,000. This is paid to certain officers for collecting statistics in addition to their regular salary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The clerk is not sure whether the item for the * Quebec bridge was passed or not.
The item for the Transcontinental railway remains over and any other items may be discussed on it. We kept it open with the distinct understanding that anything else could be discussed on it.

I understood from the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that the items for the Intercolonial railway and Quebec bridge were to stand over. I do not wish to commit myself for the member for Hamilton in any way if these items are allowed to pass.

We have gone through the Intercolonial for two or three hours, and if we left it stand now fifty hon. members may discuss it. I may have to bring back my staff and the whole matter be gone into again.

I would suggest that on the understanding the minister leaves an item over in order that discussion may take place on any point in his estimates if any member wishes to discuss any of these items. It would be only fair on account of the deputy minister being about to leave the department, that the member should give notice to the minister of what questions he wanted answered so that the rest of the staff could get the answer. It would simplify matters.

The member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) told me that the Intercolonial railway would stand over and also the Quebec bridge. The Transcontinental railway item was not touched at all. He said, however, that in dealing with these items it would not be expected that discussion would be raised that would require the presence of the deputy. They were not to go into details although there might be some broad matters on which discussion could take place.

Suppose we leave the Transcontinental, and any discussion that any hon. gentleman wants to take up on any other item of my estimates can be fully discussed on the one item of the Transcontinental. We will hare a full understanding that they can discuss anything they like.
And any information about any other item on notice?
On notice I shall be glad to give any information.
The Quebec bridge is passed.

Let the member for Hamilton and the minister settle that.
